nodes.role: Builds the portable package on demand (workflow_dispatch or a `v*` tag) by running Build App.bat itself on a Windows runner, proves the frozen executable answers in both of its modes, prints the build-info file and uploads the package as the run's artifact for seven days.
nodes.notes: Decision 78. It runs the batch file rather than re-implementing the build, because a second copy of the build is the one that drifts; tests/test_build.py refuses a workflow that names PyInstaller, the packager or the copy itself. The batch file pauses for a person at every exit, so it reads one documented switch that skips the waits, named in its own header and set here. The two smoke checks run the frozen executable, not the source: `list` with the shell's two environment variables set, which must answer JSON rather than a traceback on an install with no clients root yet, and one dry pass over a scratch clients root tests/samples.py builds, which walks filing, routing, scanning and drafting. Where the package landed is read back out of the batch file's own OUT/PLATFORM/ARCH and app/package.json's two names, so no path here is a second copy of one. Not on push: a freeze, an npm install, an Electron download and a few hundred megabytes of artifact are not what a commit should cost.

nodes.role: CI: the triggers, the concurrency rule and two jobs that both call .github/workflows/gate.yml — `linux`, a matrix of the floor interpreter and the office's on every pull request and every push to main, and `windows`, the office's interpreter on pushes to main and on pull requests labelled `windows`. It has no steps of its own.
nodes.notes: The map check is the point. docs/repo-map.md is what agents read instead of re-scanning, its freshness is guarded by test_the_committed_map_is_current, and this workflow is what makes that guard run without anyone remembering to. Every step always reports, so a stale map and a failing test surface in the same run. Windows is checked because the firm's machine is Windows and the held lock, the atomic replace and the Windows-only tests behave differently there; the python-version lines are pinned to pyproject's floor and to [tool.office] by guards. Decision 78: the matrix carries the interpreter the office runs beside that floor, because the package is frozen on the office's Python and a suite that has never run there proves nothing about it; the rows are written out one at a time rather than crossed so the floor stays one readable literal for the guard that pins it. Decision 122: a Windows minute is billed at twice a Linux one, so the two Windows rows were four fifths of the price of a run, and a series that pushes three to five times per pull request re-ran them every time — while the gate that precedes every push already runs on Windows, so those jobs repeated a check just made. A pull request now runs Linux only; Windows runs on every push to main, where it is the safety net nobody can skip, and on a pull request that asks for it with the `windows` label (`labeled` joins the pull-request triggers so labelling an open one starts the run). Windows on the floor interpreter is run nowhere, because the floor is a language-version check and Linux makes it. The steps moved out to gate.yml in the same decision: a job's own `if:` is evaluated before a matrix is expanded and cannot see the `matrix` context, so this could not be one matrix with a condition on its Windows rows, and two jobs that each wrote the steps out would be two copies of the gate. Windows is now skipped as a whole on a pull request that did not ask - never started, never billed, and reported as skipped rather than as a check that passed. A Windows-only regression in an unlabelled pull request is found by main's run; the gate and the package build both carry a timeout, so a hung job stops costing after it instead of after GitHub's six hours.

nodes.role: The gate's steps, written once: the test suite, the linter, `repo_map.py check`, `vocab_report.py check` and `node --check` on the three Electron files, on whichever runner and interpreter the caller names. Called by both of ci.yml's jobs.
nodes.notes: Decision 122. `on: workflow_call` with two required string inputs, os and python-version; the job carries timeout-minutes: 30, the ceiling that stops a hung job (the longest job yet measured is 12.5 minutes). It exists because a job's own `if:` cannot see the matrix, which makes ci.yml two jobs rather than one conditional matrix - and the steps written out in each of them would be two copies of the gate, the second one to drift. Its job is named for the runner and the interpreter it was given, so the check names read as they did before the split. Every step after the suite reports whatever the suite did, and keeps its point: a stale map and a failing test are separate problems, and seeing both in one run beats finding the second after fixing the first. Decision 137 (B3): every action is pinned by a full commit SHA with its tag beside it (tests/test_build.py holds every workflow to it).

nodes.role: No generative AI ever reads a client financial document. Every routing and status decision comes from deterministic rules in the manifest.
Nothing is ever sent. The system drafts client emails and stops. There is no SMTP, no mail client and no network call in the reminder or scheduling path.

Nothing is guessed. A document is filed only when exactly one request accepts it - or, when one document names several forms as itself, when each of those forms is accepted by exactly one request. Ambiguous, contested and unrecognized files go to 00 - Needs Review for a person - misfiling a tax document is worse than not filing it.

Originals are never altered. Files are moved byte for byte under their own names out of Drop files here into the client's folder for the year; all work happens on copies, and every move is recorded in the record.
Package docstring listing every component, and STANDING_RULES - the four rules worded once.
nodes.notes: Imports nothing of the package at load time since decision 99: the re-exports of the manifest and scaffold APIs (thirteen names no file in tracker/, tools/, tests/ or the entry point consumed) are gone, and with them the package's one load-time cycle (this package -> tracker/manifest.py -> from tracker import ledger). Its module list names the manifest as the request list - its schema, validation, and its reading from and writing to the record - and the scanner as an orchestrator that records rather than writes back (decision 104). There is no load-time cycle left to name: tests/test_layers.py pins the layer of every module and that no load-time import points upward. Every cycle the derived edges show closes through an import at call time (the map labels those separately), and tracker/filer.py <-> tracker/scanner.py inside _rescan() is the deliberate one. Standing rule 1 still says 'deterministic rules in the manifest': the manifest is the request list, and its home changed with decision 104, not the word.

nodes.role: The JSON command layer the desktop app talks to; COMMANDS is the list, and the module docstring is pinned to it. Since decision 104 it owns the request-list editor's words (EDITOR_* labels, RULES_SAVED, NOTHING_CHANGED, LEARNED_NOTE) and the edit command that saves the list and the engagement's details as one recorded event. Decision 113 added the unlearn command and the editor's two words for taking a taught keyword back (UNLEARN_LABEL, UNLEARNED_NOTE). Decision 130: create, rollover, edit, assign, hand-over (both households), dismiss, unfile and restore refresh the client README of the household they changed through filer.refresh_household_readme(), once the action has succeeded - a refused action refreshes nothing.
nodes.notes: Every command prints one JSON object and returns an exit code - errors are JSON too, never a traceback. This is the only module the Electron app knows about. The create path validates rows with the same sentences the manifest's validation uses, and never leaves a half-built engagement behind: create_engagement() validates whole before a line is written, and on any later failure _undo_create() removes the folder first and then drops the store row in its own try, so a store that cannot be reached masks nothing and keeps no folder. list/priors use the same discovery as the scheduled run; create and rollover record the details from the wizard's client/link/due (rollover carries client, sender, firm and reminders, never last year's link or due); assign files a parked document by a person's choice and re-scans. unlock clears a stale lock; state carries the lock; templates carries each form's tax year and create names a new-client engagement from client, year and form when no name is given. create takes the tax year (calendar default) and shifts catalog rows to it; rollover writes Rolled From so the prior retires; priors report superseded_by. scan is run_engagement() with reminders=REMINDERS_NEVER - the app's button and the scheduled job make the same pass. The clients root comes from tracker.settings (settings, set-root, install-schedule commands); the wizard never writes Engagement Name, and reads the firm from settings.firm(). install-schedule works in the packaged app too. ENGAGEMENT_FLAG with nothing after it, or an empty folder, gets the same sentence as no flag; once a root is set the folder must lie under it. assign takes the lock twice on purpose (file, then re-scan). _vocab() hands the renderer every word it shows - the app carries no Python vocabulary of its own. Decision 55: _under_root() checks containment whenever a root is set. Decision 67: a blank name falls back to the client's name sanitised. Decision 68: _tax_year() bounds the year on create and rollover alike, through manifest.check_tax_year() (decision 72). Decision 75: a pass made from the app is on the record the scheduled run leaves - _record_pass() appends the run log's line and redraws the status page. Decision 76: dismiss records that no request asks for a parked document and does not re-scan; _vocab() carries the decision under the key 'dismissed', not the word. Decision 77: unfile sends one filed document back for review. Decision 82: state's index rows carry evidence as data (_evidence_payload()). Decision 84: state carries 'review' - tracker.review.triage() over the rows state has already loaded, serialised by _triage_payload(). Decision 86: create records the wizard's catalog choice in the details; _state() ships it (_info_payload() is asdict() over EngagementInfo). Decision 89: _state() ships view: {state, path} from tracker.view.view_state(). Decision 91: paths['view'] is an .html file and _vocab()['view'] carries the button's own label. Decision 102: standing_rules() fills rule 2 from records.THE_RECORD; _state() calls filer.ensure() before reading the rows, so showing an engagement stays a read. DECISION 104: the edit command takes {items, engagement} from the editor, converts each row with manifest.item_from_fields() (each refusal naming its row), refuses any engagement key outside records.ENGAGEMENT_EDITABLE by name, and saves through manifest.save_rules(), replying with what changed, what was removed, which details moved, whether anything was recorded, and the warnings; a detail sent blank is cleared and one left out keeps its recorded value; a refusal is the usual error sentence and nothing is recorded. _state() gained 'rules' (the person's rows as stored - WITHOUT the keywords filings taught, so the editor never turns a taught word into a typed one), 'learned' (those keywords, keyed by the row's identifier) and 'warnings' (manifest.check_rules()); 'engagement' is the details from the record; paths lost the workbook. _vocab() gained 'columns' (each column's key, header and help from manifest.COLUMNS and COLUMN_HELP) and 'editor' (every word the editor shows, the details' fields with which are editable, the yes/no words, the two one-character values and the floors the number inputs take their minimum from); the check command and the Carried Forward sheet's name left with the things they named. DECISION 112: _state() reads store.document_seqs() once and hangs each row's sequence number beside it - on every 'index' row and on every 'review' item (_triage_payload takes the mapping) - never inside the row, because it is the record's bookkeeping and not a fact about the document. _cmd_assign, _cmd_dismiss and _cmd_unfile read spec['seq'] through _seq_of() and refuse a spec without one by NO_SEQ (a ManifestError): the app is always drawn from state, so a caller with no version is a caller with no view. _cmd_assign also computes the shortlist itself - _shortlist_now() reads the index, finds the row with filer.find_parked() and asks review.shortlist_for() over load_manifest() - and hands the identifiers to the filer, which imports neither; its payload gains 'overrode_shortlist'. This module is L4 and imports both, so the computation belongs here; the seq check under the lock is what makes a row that moved in between never get the handed-in shortlist written. DECISION 113: the unlearn command takes {identifier, keyword} from the editor, records one keyword_unlearned through manifest.unlearn_keyword() and then re-scans the engagement the way assign does (its own lock; a ScanLockedError becomes scan_note), because the request's rules just moved and a copy that passed only on that word should regress now rather than on Saturday. _vocab()['editor'] gained unlearn_label and unlearned_note - the button beside each taught keyword and the sentence after it - and the renderer types neither. Decision 117: _info_from_spec() and _info_payload() read records.DATE_FIELDS rather than naming the due date, _vocab()['editor']['date_fields'] tells the editor which boxes are dates, and rollover.with_default_dates() fills a blank Filing Deadline and Due Date from the form's own table on create and on rollover - so the reminder's ladder works without a person typing a date, and what a person typed is never written over. settings and set-root carry the firm's phone beside its name, and _vocab()['settings'] carries that box's label, its sentence and the number as recorded; _reminder_payload() takes the index rows state has already read, so the card shows the parked-file hold the draft day will. DECISION 110: _state() gains 'moved', its own list beside 'review' rather than a column on the index - one entry per FILE_MOVED row with the row's sequence number, the home the record put the copy at, where its bytes are now (None for a row whose bytes are nowhere under the firm's folder) and, only where the copy sits inside some request's folder or a subfolder of one, which request that is, matched by scaffold.assign_folders(), the same answer the filer files by. The restore command is _cmd_restore(), the third review action beside assign and unfile and the only new one: it takes the row's seq like the others and returns what the put-back found (moved_home, copied_from_original, already_home, parked_as) beside the rewritten row. _vocab()['review_labels'] carries the card's every word - RESTORE_LABEL, KEEP_LABEL, SEND_TO_REVIEW_LABEL, MOVED_HEADING, MOVED_SUMMARY and MOVED_NOWHERE, the word for a copy that is nowhere - so the renderer types none of them, and _shortlist_now() finds a moved row too, because keep-it-here goes through the same assign command and the same picker. DECISION 114: _vocab()['review_labels'] carries the review card's second rendering too - ACCEPT_LABEL, SKIP_LABEL, OPEN_IN_LIST_LABEL, the two words the toggle between the renderings shows (CARD_MODE_LABEL, LIST_MODE_LABEL) and CARD_POSITION, the pattern the card's position line is filled from. The heading over the card's suggestion is SUGGESTED_HEADING, the list's own: one queue, one word for a suggestion. No command is added and no payload changes - the cards are a rendering of the 'review' list this module already ships, and Accept is the assign command the list's File it makes. Decision 123: that function is no longer defined here - it moved to tracker.rollover, beside the carry rule that clears the dates, because the module's command line built engagements without it; create and rollover import it and are otherwise unchanged. Decision 118 added the reminder and approve commands and everything the Reminder card shows. reminder reads the record and the draft file and regenerates the letter in memory at whatever stage the toggle stands on - no lock, nothing written, and a held reminder answers with no letter at all; approve takes the engagement lock, refuses a stale panel by the fingerprint of the text it showed, writes the shown text (or approves an edited file as it stands), sets any other draft aside and records one draft_approved event. _vocab() carries the card's every word, the four stages with the palette key each carries and where each spends its emphasis, and page.PALETTE itself, so the renderer types neither a word nor a colour; state's paths now name the draft file, because the shell opens only paths this map holds. Decision 126 added two commands and the sharing words: roll-household rolls every ticked return of a household's open year through rollover.roll_household() and answers with the rolled, the skipped with their sentences, the retired by their labels and the state of the first return it made; mark-shared records one sharing_confirmed event on the household's record under its lock, refusing while the inbox link is blank (SHARE_LINK_FIRST) because that is the one part of the checklist the tracker can see was done. SHARING_CHECKLIST, SHARING_HEADING, SHARING_NOTE, MARK_SHARED_LABEL, SHARED_ON_LINE, NOT_YET_SHARED_LINE and ROLLOVER_UNTICKED_NOTE are the API's words; create hands the filled checklist back with a household's FIRST return and with no other, and state['household'] carries shared_on and the same filled lines until it is given. propose-spellings is the twenty-third command and a read: it proposes the spellings a document might print one name in and records nothing, because what a return matches on is what a person ticked (decision 128). create refuses a return with nobody on it. Decision 129 added the feed words (FEEDS_LABEL, FEEDS_LINE, FED_BY_LINE, ADD_FEED_LABEL, FEED_WARNING, RETURN_WARNING, HAND_OVER_LABEL, NOT_FED), the feeds field on edit-household, the feeds and fed_by the household card is drawn from, and assign's optional target - which hands the document to a return the drop folder feeds and refuses any other by name. The review of that build added the hand-over modal's own two words (HAND_OVER_RETURN_LABEL, HAND_OVER_REQUEST_LABEL), which the page had been borrowing from the household heading and the editor's title, and gave _cmd_scan the same walk of the practice the card uses (_the_practice), so Run now sorts against the feed list exactly as the scheduled pass does rather than against the household's own returns alone; since decision 132 a root that cannot be walked is the runner's NO_PRACTICE, the reply's run error, and nothing is sorted. HANDED_OVER_LINE (review_labels.handed_over) is what the page says after a hand-over: the row here is released. Decision 131: _state() carries 'room' (room_for over the list it already loaded), 'room_note' (ROOM_SHORT filled, or '' - information the return's page shows, never a warning) and appends only ROOM_PARKS to the warnings; set-root answers 'short_of_room' - every working return short of room under the new root, in label order, with its numbers and filled sentences (one walk; the one time room is measured outside a pass) - and records the root regardless; the editor's save (_cmd_edit) refuses with PATH_TOO_LONG a CHANGED or new row whose canonical path passes 260, and never a row the person did not touch; install-schedule writes the job from settings_dir() and replies 'settings'. _vocab()['room'] holds the heading and the two sentences. Decision 137: create refuses a household folder that exists without a record (HOUSEHOLD_NOT_OURS, the misfit rule stated at the door) and makes every folder through fsio.make_new_folders(), so a failure undoes only what this call made (_undo_made); rollover the same. _under_root() and so _engagement_dir() refuse when no clients root is set, and _engagement_dir() names a return by its place (four levels under the root, under a year) - a year or household folder is refused (NOT_A_RETURN) rather than read one level too high. _feeds_from_spec() refuses a feed whose household or return line the sanitiser would change. Review fixes: _undo_made() removes whole only the folders a call owns (its return, a household whose record it wrote) and a year folder only when empty; create drops a household's pre-137 non-web link with rollover.carried_link and returns link_dropped; the reminder card carries link_dropped.

nodes.role: Tier 3: extract text (pdfplumber / openpyxl / plain text, OCR for a scan or a photo) and test it against the row's keyword and date rules. extract() is the one reading of a document, used by the router and the scanner alike; ContentCache keeps the verdicts - in the store, per engagement, since decision 107.
nodes.notes: The cache stores verdicts only - pass/fail, the reason, and the Evidence behind them, all of it the firm's own words. Extracted client text is never persisted. Only the first MAX_PAGES pages of a PDF are read, text or OCR - the identifying words are up front and a long ledger used to stall a run. Verdicts are keyed by the file's content digest and the row's rules fingerprint (CACHE_VERSION, carried on every row; a row at another version is ignored and dropped), with a per-path memo of size/mtime/digest so an unchanged file is not re-hashed: the same bytes are read twice in this system, once as a drop the router routes and once as the working copy the scanner checks, and a verdict the router reached is the verdict the scanner finds. extract(ocr=False) hands a scan back with needs_ocr set so the router can try the file's name first; extract_by_ocr() finishes the reading. The CLI (python -m tracker.content_check <engagement> <file>) prints what the document says and which rows accept it, writing no cache. DECISION 107 - THE CACHE LEFT THE SYNCED FOLDER: ContentCache(engagement_dir) loads the engagement's memos and verdicts from the store's two tables (store.cached_verdicts()) once, works in memory as it always did, and save() writes what it learned and forgot through store.remember_verdicts() - one immediate transaction of the store's own, under the engagement lock, never store.record(), because a verdict is a derivation of the bytes and the rules and not an event; a pass killed mid-save leaves the previous rows. ContentCache() with no engagement is memory only (the CLI's, a test's) and its save() touches nothing. The engagement must already be in the store or the constructor refuses by name. The JSON cache file that used to sit in the engagement folder is never read; RETIRED_CACHE_FILENAME survives only for the filer's tidy-up, which removes it. THE STEP-0 RE-RUN'S FINDING: decision 105 had kept a two-form split's second verdict in the cache alone, so a rebuilt store read the second copy the ordinary way and failed it - the cache was carrying a decision, not a derivation. own_forms(text) is now the one reading of which forms a page counts as its own (the set of self-named forms when MULTI_FORM_FAMILIES or more families print their own name, else None; the constant moved here from the router, which re-exports it for one release); _check_uncached() reads through it, so the scan's miss verdict is the router's kept verdict for every page, split included, and a delete-and-rebuild leaves every status byte-identical. _evidence_from_json() takes a tuple as well as a list, so a verdict read back in the pass that kept it carries its evidence. Decision 55: contains_keyword() treats a hyphen-joined form variant as part of the form's name (1098 never matches 1098-T); a verdict that is the machine's (no OCR, OCR failed) is transient and never cached. Decision 57: FORM_VARIANTS is the one list of each form's real variants; _JOINER is what may sit between a number and its variant or a keyword's words; the text-layer floor is per page; CACHE_VERSION 3. Decision 60: _seams() lets a keyword typed w2 find W-2; no letters or digits means no keyword. Decision 62: says() is contains_keyword() as content evidence - a form number counts only within TITLE_CHARS; _seams() reads plurals, keeps numbers out of amounts, takes any apostrophe. Decision 63: dominant_forms() - a form number counts in the text when it is in the title or is the number the document mentions most; form <anything> is a form number. Decision 64: dominant_forms() weighs a mention by its shape - a form names itself with its year or revision and another form in a sentence. Decision 66: the title is weighed the same way (_title_forms(); _REFERENCE_BEFORE marks a form quoted after attach/forms/see/of/on/and/or), a number outside FORM_VARIANTS is a mention only after Form, a keyword's words sit on one line or wrap as a heading from a line's start (_WRAPPING_JOINER, _LINE_START), a sheet's cells are tab-separated within a row; CACHE_VERSION 5. Decision 67: what comes before a form is read before what follows it (attach Form 1098 (2025) is a reference); a title naming _LIST_OF_FORMS or more forms names none; the title window is measured on the lower-cased text; _LINE_START admits a bullet, a pipe or a rule. Decision 68: _LIST_OF_FORMS counts families (_FAMILY), so a consolidated 1099 is one family's document; _REFERENCE_BEFORE stays on one line. Decision 69: a form number set off by a dash is a reference (_REFERENCE_AFTER), a dash before the year is still dated (_SELF_AFTER), and _REFERENCE_BEFORE reads across a line break again. Decision 73: says() weighs where a plain keyword is said, not only that it is there - an occurrence that is a menu line's title (_menu_tails: a form number and the title a dash or a comma sets off from it are one reference) or what an ask-word asked for (_asked_for: attach, provide, send, see and their kin, governing the rest of their own sentence and the line a request wraps on to) is the page talking about a document rather than being one, and one occurrence that is neither is enough. A dash-set-off form that heads its line with a year beside it, where the title window holds no second such line and no ask precedes it, names itself (_titles_its_own_line), so a payer's substitute form is not read as a checklist. A form number after a comma continues a list (_LIST_CONTINUES), and enclosed/enclosure/enclosures/re: join _REFERENCE_BEFORE, which now reads a colon between the word and the form. any_keyword_matched() answers the router's question 'did this row's keywords match, apart from the year?'. CACHE_VERSION 6. Decision 82: a verdict keeps the evidence behind it. Evidence(rule, term, where, page) is the one shape - EVIDENCE_RULES (required, any, date, filename, refused) and EVIDENCE_PLACES (title, first_page, footer, deep) are the named values, imported by the router, the index and the app's vocabulary and retyped nowhere. The Evidence record, those two lists and the cell format that format_evidence() writes and parse_evidence() reads now live in tracker/records.py (decision 100) and are re-exported here for one release; what stays here is the reading of a document that produces them. says() became a thin wrapper over _says_where(), which reaches the same verdict by the same reading and also says where the word was found (_where_said(): the title window first, then a page's last _FOOTER_LINES non-blank lines, then the rest of page 1, then deep), so no placement moved. evaluate_rules() puts an Evidence per matched rule on ContentResult.evidence, on a failing verdict too, and the reason sentence is untouched; the date rule records the row's Period, not the regex it derives and not a word of the document. format_evidence()/parse_evidence() are the one owner of the index cell's compact form (term@where:page rule, candidates joined by '; '), and the page is left off when it is 0. CACHE_VERSION 7, because a version-6 verdict read back would claim a verdict with no reason behind it. nodes.role: Sorts the household's one inbox across every return of its open year (decision 125): moves each original out of it into the client's folder for the year, untouched, copies a renamed working file into Prepared/... or 00 - Needs Review, and records every move in the engagement's own record - the journal and the store together, in one transaction per decision. Owns read_index(), which answers from the store, and ensure(), which brings the store up to the journal and says whether it is current. Decision 130: received_for() reads each return's index and request list once and returns what the client README acknowledges as plain data (Filed/File Moved = Received once per request satisfied, by request label - an also-filed copy names a request only by its exact folder name or identifier + LABEL_SEPARATOR, else Other document; Needs Review = Under Review, counted by day; nothing else shown), and refresh_household_readme() - the one call the pass, the rollover and every app action make - reads scaffold.readme_returns() once for both received_for() and scaffold.write_readme(), under a per-household README lock (README_LOCK_FILENAME in the private household folder; busy past README_LOCK_WAIT_SECONDS = skip with a log line), and never raises. Since decision 128 the pass also asks whose each document is, between the request lists' acceptances and the exactly-one rule.
nodes.notes: Content-hash de-duplication makes re-runs no-ops. _sort_one() decides one preserved original's fate against a _SortContext built once per run (the request list, the index so far, folders, claimed names, the run's caches). The verdicts the router reaches while sorting are written to the engagement's verdicts in the store (content_check.ContentCache over store.remember_verdicts(), keyed by content; decision 107), so the scan that follows finds them under the working copy's name and never reads the document twice; a dry run saves nothing. The tidy-up at the end of a real pass also removes the retired JSON cache file and any temp file beside it (_remove_the_retired_cache(), by RETIRED_CACHE_FILENAME) - nothing reads it, and the removal is said once on FileReport.attention (RETIRED_CACHE_REMOVED) - on the console, in the app's warnings and counted on the practice page - for that pass only. Originals are moved byte for byte under their own names and never altered. Each drop is handled on its own: a drop that cannot be moved is left in place for the next run, a drop that fails after it was preserved is recorded as Needs Review with the error, and the record is written in a finally block so nothing moved into the year's folder is ever unrecorded. Runs under the engagement lock - its own when it is called alone, the pass's when runner.run_engagement() is holding one - taken before the request list, the record or the drop folder is read. Files the client drops straight into the visible year folder are filed and indexed in place; a re-sent document whose working copy vanished from Prepared/ is re-filed rather than called a duplicate; a Document renamed in the editor keeps filing into the folder that already holds its files (assign_folders, not folder_name_for); empty client folders are cleared after sorting. assign_review_file() is the person's counterpart to file_household_drops(): moves the parked copy under the canonical name (or copies from the client's folder for the year if it is gone), rewrites the index row as Filed with the ASSIGNED_BY_PERSON reason, records the keyword a person typed in the same call, all under the engagement lock. The IndexEntry record and INDEX_LAYOUT live in tracker/records.py (decision 100). HISTORY, kept as history: until decision 102 the index was a workbook rewritten whole on every pass, and decisions 54, 56, 58, 59, 61, 65, 66, 67, 68, 69 and 72 are thirteen readings of what that cost - a snapshot sidecar that outlived its workbook, a deferred write, a stale workbook, a header row a sort had moved, a renamed tab, a column inserted at A; what survives of them here is the reading of bytes (replaced_in_pbc() decides by bytes alone; _copy_whole() leaves no half-written copy; every move is a rename in _move_whole(), because shutil.move copied a held-open drop truncated into the year's folder; what lies behind a junction is not a drop; a name Windows cannot open is reported every pass; a row recorded without its bytes is tied to them only while its working copy and its original agree, UNTIED_IN_PBC; a recorded original that has left the year's folder is said every pass, MISSING_IN_PBC, and where a stray carries its bytes the row follows the file, MOVED_IN_PBC; REPLACED_IN_PBC and UNTIED_IN_PBC are FileReport.attention, not errors; a parked path a later row records is the later row's; assign reuses an earlier attempt's copy first and leaves an annotated parked copy, saying so). Decision 76: dismiss_review_file() rewrites a parked row NOT_REQUESTED with the DISMISSED_BY_PERSON reason and moves nothing; _find_parked() takes a dismissed row too, so filing it is the undo. Decision 111: a re-send is judged by the earlier row's decision - the content hash says which row holds those bytes and that row's decision says what this drop is. A filed row with its copy in place, a row parked for a person, and a row whose copy is not where the record put it all make it a Duplicate, and the sentence names which (DUPLICATE_OF_FILED, DUPLICATE_OF_PARKED, DUPLICATE_OF_MOVED, and DUPLICATE_OF_UNCOPIED of a row with no working copy to name: saying 'already filed as' of a parked copy told the Index a document still waiting was done); a filed row whose copy is gone is decision 24's re-file; a row a person set aside is routed like any other drop - Not requested is a decision about one document on one day, not a standing rule - and files where exactly one request now accepts it, else parks with a FRESH copy of its own (never _existing_copy, or filing one row would carry the other row's file away), the reason quoting the earlier decision whole (RESENT_AFTER_SET_ASIDE) so the row is triaged, counted by reminder.count_needs_review() and read by a person. Decision 77: unfile_document() is the way back - the working copy returns to 00 - Needs Review under the client's own name, the row is rewritten NEEDS_REVIEW with the UNFILED_BY_PERSON reason, and the engagement is re-scanned (outside the lock, which the scan takes for itself); a working copy that is no longer the row's bytes is left and said out loud (LEFT_FILED). Decision 82: IndexEntry.evidence is the last column, written through records.format_evidence() and read back through records.parse_evidence(); a person's decision leaves it alone. Decision 87: every decision is appended to the record through tracker/ledger.py by one rule, _rows_changed(), read off the rows themselves. DECISION 102 - THE INDEX MOVED INTO THE RECORD: read_index() takes the engagement folder and reads the store's documents table, in the index's own order, after store.follow_the_journal(); _record() is the one write, every event a decision produces in a single store.record() call, and the rollback that puts a moved file back asks _the_record_holds(). The migration that read a legacy folder's index workbook into the journal once, and the request-list import of decision 103 that read the sheet once a pass and journalled its differences, both LEFT WITH DECISION 104 and are set aside outside the tree in Retired - Excel manifest: ensure() is now the store's top-up and the three words that say whether it describes the engagement, it writes nothing in the folder, and every caller drops the flag that used to keep a dry run from migrating. clients_root_of() is store.root_for() under its old name. _storable() keeps only the refusal of a name UTF-8 cannot hold (the journal is UTF-8 JSON); a control character in a POSIX name files again, because the refusal of one existed only because a workbook is XML. A person's filing records its keyword in the SAME store.record() call as the row (_record()'s also), because the filing and what it taught are one decision. THE DELIBERATE CYCLE: _rescan() imports tracker/scanner.py at call time so a person's filing is scanned the moment it lands, and the scanner imports this module's index reader at call time; neither runs at load. DECISION 112 - A PERSON'S ACTION IS JUDGED AGAINST THE RECORD IT WAS MADE ON: assign_review_file(), dismiss_review_file() and unfile_document() each take seq=, the row's sequence number as the person saw it, and _refuse_if_stale() compares it with store.document_seqs() immediately after the row is found - inside the lock, before a byte is read or a file is touched - raising StaleRowError (a FilingError, so the API's one except turns it into the app's sentence) with STALE_ROW, which names what the record now says. seq=None is a caller with no view (a script, a test) and skips the check; the by-name refusal is asked first and is a different question. assign_review_file() also takes shortlist=, the identifiers the evidence pointed at, computed by the caller that drew the card: a pick off a non-empty shortlist writes OVERRODE_SHORTLIST into the row's reason after the ASSIGNED_BY_PERSON prefix (the scanner's acceptance still keys on startswith) and comes back on AssignResult.overrode_shortlist; an empty shortlist is never an override. This module does not import tracker/review.py - that would be a second call-time cycle beside the deliberate one - which is why the shortlist is handed in. find_parked() and find_filed() are public for the same reason (the underscored names kept for one release), so the API finds exactly the row this module will act on. DECISION 109 - EVERY WORKING COPY IS PROVED AGAINST THE RECORD EACH PASS: _prove_working_copies() is one walk of Prepared/ per pass, under the pass's lock, between the PBC sweep and the known-bytes map, and it has four outcomes and only these. A copy where the record put it holding the row's digest is proved and nothing is written. A copy that is absent or holds other bytes, whose bytes turn up at a path no row names, makes its row FILE_MOVED - a decision on the document, never a Status (the owner's rule, 2026-09-19) - with home kept in prepared_location and where the bytes are now in a sentence (MOVED_SENTENCE, MOVED_GONE_SENTENCE), read back by moved_to() through records.as_pattern(); the scanner reads that row and writes the request's note. Where more than one file no row names holds those bytes, the row keeps the wanderer it already names (_spend_a_stray()'s preferred): the copy that sorts first is not the copy a person moved, and decision 110's put-it-back follows the sentence. A FILE_MOVED row whose every claimed location holds its bytes again is FILED once more (NEEDS_REVIEW where the row names no request - which of the two parked decisions it was is not guessable), MOVED_BACK_SENTENCE. A file under a request folder or the review folder that no row names and no row's bytes match is UNRECORDED_COPY on FileReport.attention, every pass, counted where it sits. THE RECORD DECIDES AND NOTHING MOVES: the fingerprint identifies, a person acts (decision 110's buttons), and a quiet pass appends nothing - one ledger.COPY_MOVED event per move, in either direction, named through _LEDGER_EVENT_FOR and _record()'s decided. A row without its bytes is never swept (decision 65) but still names its copy, so that copy is not called unrecorded; a placeholder is never read; a Duplicate row is not followed. _copy_whole() now proves its target against the digest it was made from and raises CopyMismatchError - decision 17's could-not-be-filed row - rather than leaving a copy nobody checked; every caller passes what it knows, and the pass's callers pass the ContentCache too, so the memo the proof leaves is the scan's hit. DECISION 110 - RECOVERY IS THE PERSON'S: restore_working_copy() is the answer to a FILE_MOVED row that needs no other place for the file to go - the bytes return to where the record put them, by moving the wanderer moved_to() names when it still holds them and by copying from the client's original when nothing under the firm's folder does - and the row goes back to what it was before it wandered, FILED where it names a request and NEEDS_REVIEW where it does not. It never overwrites (a file already at home that is not this document stays exactly where it is; this document's copy goes to review under the client's own name and the row parks naming both, PUT_BACK_REFUSED), never deletes (a home that already holds these bytes leaves the wanderer where it is for a person to remove, PUT_BACK_ALREADY) and never guesses (the row's sequence number first, every byte it is about to move second, the move third, and a refused record puts back exactly what moved). Every location the row claims is put back, not the Prepared Location column alone: the sweep names the first location that failed, and a page decision 94 filed under several requests has a copy in each, each remade from the one just put back. One event whatever the click found, ledger.RESTORED_BY_PERSON, because the row it carries says which. The other two answers are the actions that already existed: keep-it-here is assign_review_file() on a moved row, where the copy that moves is the wanderer and the request may be the folder's own or another the person picks; send-it-to-review is unfile_document(), where the wanderer is the copy that goes back and a row whose bytes are nowhere is copied from the original. Both refuse a row with copies under several requests by name (SEVERAL_COPIES_REFUSAL) and point at put-it-back. find_parked() and find_filed() take accepting=, the decisions the action will have beyond the ones they were written for, so those two reach a FILE_MOVED row and dismiss_review_file() still refuses one by name (decision 76); find_moved() is their shape over FILE_MOVED itself. DECISION 119 - AN INTERRUPTED MOVE IS FINISHED FROM THE RECORD, NEVER GUESSED: before the first file operation of any decision - a pass's copy, a person's filing, unfiling or put-back - _intend() appends ledger.MOVING under the lock, keyed by the row's own ledger key, carrying the operations in order with the digest each end should hold, the row the decision will record, the event that will complete it, who decided and (for a drop's own move, which has no row yet) the day the run began; _do_op() is the one place a plan is carried out, by the decision and by the recovery alike, so a move a recovery makes is the move the decision would have made. _finish_interrupted_moves() runs at the start of every pass, under the lock, after the index is read and before the digests of rows recorded without them are filled in, before the client's folder is read for strays and before the sweep - so a person's half-made filing is finished and recorded as theirs rather than swept up as a copy somebody dragged. Each operation is checked by bytes and finished where reality matches; the intent's row is then recorded as the intent said, with the events that travelled with it, dated the day the person decided. Where a destination holds other bytes nothing there is touched and the row parks with reasons.INTERRUPTED_MOVE naming it (interrupted_at() and interrupted_note() read the sentence back for the scanner, as moved_to() does 109's); where neither end holds the bytes the row parks with INTERRUPTED_MOVE_LOST; either way the copy a person acts on is the one waiting in review if there is one, else a fresh one from the client's original. _refuse_if_a_move_is_open() refuses all four person actions while an intent is open here, before 112's freshness check, because the next pass - or Run now - finishes it. A refused record rolls back as it always did and appends ledger.MOVE_ABANDONED so the next pass does not finish forward a move the record would not take. RECORD_PRESERVE_INTENTS is the one switch: the pass's own move into the client's folder is already finished by decision 23, and its intent buys only the received date. _plan_working_copy() took over from the filer's old one-step copy helper: deciding where a working copy goes and making it are two steps now, because what will happen has to be written down before it does. refuse_a_path_past_the_limit() lives here since decision 126: the deepest thing a return ever holds is a working copy this module writes, and both creation (tracker.api) and the household rollover (tracker.rollover, at a layer below the API) measure it before a folder is made. The name tier (decision 128) runs inside file_household_drops: one reading per drop, then check_name() per accepting return against that return's own people. A named request keeps its acceptance only where the name confirms, an unnamed one keeps it where the name is merely absent, and any return whose page names somebody on another return of the household is dropped. What is left goes to the exactly-one rule; a list the name emptied parks in the home return with reasons.NAME_NOT_ON_PAGE, NAMES_ANOTHER_RETURN or NO_PEOPLE_ON_FILE, in that order. A filing by hand may teach one spelling, recorded as one rules_changed event inside the filing's own transaction exactly as a taught keyword is. A list the name emptied parks in the first return that ACCEPTED the document (decision 125's home), the first return by folder order only where nothing accepted it at all. Both of decision 111's re-send roads - a row a person set aside, a filed row whose working copy is gone - are name-checked the same way inside _sort_one() before they file, or the check could be walked round by sending a document twice. Decision 129 widened the sort from the household's own returns to its feed list, and decision 132 re-specified it: file_household_drops(inbox, originals, own=, fed=) takes the two lists by name, judges own returns first (the bytes are asked of the records in that order - the record closest to the drop decides - while the locks were taken in the global one), a document nobody may file always parks in a home return (_the_home), and a filing into any return goes through _file_into() - ONE SHAPE FOR THE PASS AND A PERSON: one intent in the TARGET's record, keyed on the row's final location, ops [move original -> resting] (only where the household differs) + [copy resting -> each working copy], then the row (FILED for the pass, ASSIGNED_BY_PERSON for a person) and its also events; nothing ever writes into another return's record. hand_over() is two intents in two records, each finished by its own household's pass with no lock it does not hold: the home's release intent first (remove the parked copy, then ledger.RELEASED with RELEASED_TO as its reason - the row leaves the index, the dropping household keeps no row), then the taking return's filing through _file_into(), its row, the home's remove and the release. A kill after the release intent alone costs the person's click (the original, named by no row, is a stray re-sorted where it lies). A PASS LEAVES ALONE AN ORIGINAL ANOTHER RECORD'S OPEN INTENT NAMES (the lead's ruling R-1): _named_by_another_records_intent() - asked only when a stray is found - reads every return of the practice (positionally, each followed to its journal first, no lock) for an open intent naming that path with those bytes as a step's source, and such a file is never re-sorted, parked or recorded - but it is said, LEFT_FOR_ANOTHER_RETURN on the first own return's attention every pass it happens (ruling R-3), so an intent that never finishes never leaves an original unmentioned; so the taking return's recovery always finishes the move and each half of a hand-over is finished by its own household's pass. _decide_across() records a reading's seconds on first (the first own return, the run the inbox's own notes ride - SPEC-127.1 9.2). Owns the event names (preserved, filed, parked, duplicate, assigned_by_person, dismissed_by_person, unfiled_by_person, bytes_recorded, keyword_learned, keyword_unlearned, scanned, rules_changed, drafted, imported, migrated; rules_imported retired - read, never written), their payload keys, append() / read_events() / fold() / statuses() / rules() / apply() / replay() / head() / read_with_head(), and the file name. Owns the event names (preserved, filed, parked, duplicate, assigned_by_person, dismissed_by_person, unfiled_by_person, bytes_recorded, keyword_learned, scanned, rules_changed, drafted, imported, migrated; rules_imported retired - read, never written), their payload keys, append() / read_events() / fold() / statuses() / rules() / apply() / replay() / head() / read_with_head(), and the file name.
nodes.notes: Decision 87 wrote it beside the files that already existed and had nothing read it; decision 88 made the readers believe it; DECISION 102 MADE IT THE INDEX; DECISION 103 THE STATUSES AND THE PERSON'S RULES; DECISION 104 THE ONLY PLACE THE RULES ARE. The fold of these lines - through tracker/store.py, which keeps the fold so that no reader pays for it twice - IS what filer.read_index() returns and what manifest.load_manifest() and manifest.load_engagement_info() answer, and nothing else holds those rows. apply() folds a rules_changed event, and the retired rules_imported an older journal carries, the same way (_apply_rules_event): the rows the event carried replace those identifiers, the ones it names as removed go, the details it carried are set; the create carries the whole list and every save only what moved, so the fold of every event is the list - which is what makes store.rebuild_engagement() able to take everything from the journal alone. RETIRED_EVENTS names what this version reads and never writes: new(), append() and store.record() refuse rules_imported by sentence (RETIRED_EVENT), and a digest an old line carries is simply not read. fold() returns rows in the index's own order, and a row that changed identity keeps the place the one it left held. What keeps it honest is the autouse fixture in tests/conftest.py: after every test a store is built from nothing and held to replay() over these lines - the documents, the statuses and the rules alike. Sits at the bottom beside tracker/locking.py and imports only it: the events are plain dicts, so each writer serialises its own rows with the function in tracker/records.py that owns that shape, and no cycle is created. One os.write of the whole line under O_APPEND then fsync, so a kill mid-append leaves at most a torn tail: read_events() ignores it and the next append() truncates it, and nothing else ever rewrites the file. O_APPEND is atomic for concurrent writers on POSIX and is not on Windows, which is why append() refuses unless locking.lock_is_held() says this process holds the engagement lock. Not SQLite: a database file a cloud client syncs is a corrupted database file. migrated is the one event that carries no row - it named the files decision 102's migration moved aside; nothing writes one since 104, and it stays readable. Rows are keyed by the original's PBC location; a row that followed an original the client moved carries the identity it left (was), so the fold drops the vacated one. fold() passes over an event name it does not know and read_events() refuses a bad line anywhere but the tail. The reminder writes files and takes no lock, so drafted is reserved; runner and api reach the writers through the filer, the scanner and the manifest and make no call of their own. Decision 115 unreserved DRAFTED: written by the pass under the lock it holds and by the reminder's CLI under one it takes, carrying ASKED_KEY (identifiers asked, in order; [] on a quiet week) or HELD_KEY (identifiers that held the draft), and FILE_KEY / FINGERPRINT_KEY when a file was written - identifiers only, never a word of the email; appended only when something moved. day_of() is the one reading of a stamp, the local day it fell on, beside stamp() the one writing. Decision 113 gave it the one fold it never had: KEYWORD_UNLEARNED is the event a person's unlearn writes, Folded.learned is identifier -> the keywords filings taught and nobody has taken back, and _apply_keyword_event() folds both - learn appends the word, or moves it last where it is already there, and unlearn removes it, so a word taught again lands last either way, which is the order the store's own ORDER BY seq gives, its insert carrying the new line's sequence number. The two folds agree by construction and not because no writer here teaches a word twice. The identifier is keyed exactly as each line spells it, because this module sits below records and may not borrow identifier_key (test_layers); the one reader that has to join two spellings of a request, store._check_learned(), folds both sides itself. So the learned table is inside store.check() at last, and the suite's rebuild-and-check fixture proves it after every test. Decision 110 added restored_by_person to ROW_EVENTS: a person put a working copy back where the record put it, one name whatever the click found, because the row the line carries says whether the bytes moved home, were copied home from the original, were already there, or were refused a home holding a different file and sent to review. Decision 119 added MOVING (not a row event) and MOVE_ABANDONED: what one decision is about to do to the disk, written before the first file operation and keyed by the row's own identity - OPS_KEY (the operations in order, each with the digest both ends should hold), ROW_KEY (the row the decision will record), EVENT_KEY_AFTER (the event that will complete it), DECIDED_BY_KEY (a pass or a person), ALSO_KEY (the events that travel with the row, a taught keyword today) and DAY_KEY (the runner's own day, carried where there is no row to carry it). They fold into Folded.intents rather than into the index: the row event that names the key closes the intent, and the abandonment closes one the record refused. Decision 118 added draft_approved beside drafted: a person read the week's draft in the app and approved it, carrying the stage, the file, that file's header fingerprint and the identifiers asked. Folded by nothing, like drafted - a fact about a week, not a row of the index - and carrying no word of the letter. Decision 126 added sharing_confirmed on the same pattern, in the household's journal: the firm's word that it shared the household with its client, folded by nothing and carrying nothing at all but the stamp, because the tracker cannot see Drive's sharing and must not record what it cannot check. tracker.store._refuse_a_malformed_line() refuses a line of it that carries anything. Decision 132 added RELEASED ({event, key, reason}, no row, the shape of MOVE_ABANDONED; not a row event): apply() removes the row under the key - and under a was, the path a row event's re-key already deletes - and closes the intent, so the dropping household of a hand-over keeps no row and the journal line alone says which return took it (REASON_KEY). RELEASE_EVENTS is RELEASED and the retired handed_over_by_person decision 129 wrote, which joins RETIRED_EVENTS: read once, folded as a release of its key, never written. Nothing an intent carries is written into another return's record any more; decision 129's ALSO_IN_KEY is gone and tracker.store refuses a moving line that carries it, by name. Decision 135: read_with_head() returns the events and the head from one read of the file; read_events() and head() are thin wrappers over the same _parse() and _digest(), so there is one parser. Whoever saves a head beside lines it applied (the store) uses read_with_head(). Decision 137 (A3): _parse_lines() keeps each event's own line bytes, chain_link() is one step of the applied chain (sha256 of the chain so far and the line), and read_with_chain() returns the events, the head and the chain after each line from one read - the store's proof that the lines it applied are still the journal's. The journal's format is unchanged.

nodes.role: One lock per engagement (LOCK_FILENAME, O_EXCL, stale after STALE_LOCK_SECONDS), held by runner.run_engagement() across a whole pass, by the filer or the scanner on its own when either is run alone, and by the manifest's two writes. EngagementLock (the open handle and its token), EngagementLockedError; engagement_lock() context manager, taken before the request list, the record or the drop folder is read.
nodes.notes: Exists because two runs on one engagement (scheduler repeat overlapping a desktop click) raced on the same originals and the loser's rows were written from a stale picture. The filer moves and records; the scanner records statuses; the manifest records a person's edit (decision 104) - all under this one lock, one protocol. Dry runs never take it. The descriptor stays open while held (Windows then refuses to delete it, so a stale-looking lock its owner still holds is refused) and release_lock() removes the file only if it still carries this run's token. RUN_TIME_LIMIT_SECONDS is the one number for how long a scheduled pass may run: tracker.scheduling renders it as the task's ExecutionTimeLimit and STALE_LOCK_SECONDS is derived above it. One machine per clients root: a lock file synced between two machines is not a lock. lock_status()/clear_stale_lock() back the app's lock notice. Decision 54: pid_alive() - a lock whose owner process is gone is stale at any age. Decision 56: the lock line carries host=; another host's pid is unknowable, never dead. Decision 59: a lock that cannot be deleted on release is marked RELEASED_LINE. Decision 102: the lock is not re-entrant - it is an O_EXCL file - so the steps a pass makes take a lock_held flag and skip taking it, and a writer that may be reached with the lock already held (manifest.save_rules(), the journal's append) asks lock_is_held() rather than taking it twice. Decision 115: the machine's name in the lock line comes from platform.node(), not from the socket module - the same name, and the package imports no network module. Decision 137 (L6): the module docstring states that the stale-lock rules rest on the one-machine rule - another host's lock is left to the age rule, whose promise is this machine's schedule's.

nodes.role: The request list: its schema, its validation, and its reading from and writing to the record. Since decision 104 the manifest IS the record's request list - the eleven accountant columns (COLUMNS, whose headers are HEADERS, each with the sentence COLUMN_HELP gives the editor) and the engagement's details - and there is no workbook. Owns RequestItem, Status, Override, item_from_fields() and validated() (the validation the sheet's loader used to make, as a function on records), load_manifest() and load_engagement_info() (the answers, from the record), create_engagement() and save_rules() (the two writes, each one rules_changed event), check_rules() (the warnings) and summarize().
nodes.notes: Every other module goes through this to touch the request list. THE OWNER RETIRED THE EXCEL MANIFEST ON 2026-09-19 (decision 104): until then the list was the workbook registry.LEGACY_MANIFEST_FILENAME names, read once a pass and journalled as it changed; now the app's editor is the only way a rule is entered, and every save is one rules_changed event through store.record() under the engagement lock - create_engagement() carries the whole list and every detail (validated before a line is written, so a refusal leaves no folder content and no store row), save_rules() carries exactly the rows that changed, whole and row included (a row's position is part of the rule, so a row moved is a row changed), the identifiers removed and the details that moved, and nothing at all when nothing did. The diff is by the identifier's exact spelling and the folds (ledger.apply and the store's) apply removals before rows and delete by that exact spelling (never SQLite's ASCII-only lower()); _refuse_a_malformed_line() refuses a rules_changed or scanned line of the wrong shape by name before a value of it reaches a table, so an identifier respelled by case is one event - the old spelling removed, the new carried - and never two rows. create_engagement() forgets the store row a folder deleted by hand left before following the new journal. The writes came back here, having left in 103, because the module that owns the schema and the validation must own the writes, or the rows in the journal would be shaped by somebody else; they reach store, ledger and locking at call time, so the module still imports tracker/records.py and nothing else at load time (tests/test_layers.py). item_from_fields() is the one parser of a row from plain values (the editor's JSON, a catalog spec, a test's dict), its refusals prefixed by where - a row number from the API, the identifier from the catalog - and it defaults NO keyword, as the sheet allowed; validated() makes the list-level checks (identifier required and folder-safe, duplicates without case because Windows folders are, the two numbers within MIN_EXPECTED_COUNT and MIN_SIZE_KB_FLOOR, NO_DATE_CHECK made blank, a typed pattern compiled, a blank one derived from the Period with date_pattern_derived set, and last check_narrowing_names()) and numbers the rows 1..n. Every path that stores rules or routes against a catalog goes through it - the two writes, tests/test_irs_forms.py, tests/test_catalog.py, tools/vocab_report.py - so the derived year check the harnesses used to get from a workbook round trip is the same check, made once. A row that comes back from the store says its pattern was derived, and both parsers read that as no pattern typed, so a list read out of the record and saved again records nothing. load_manifest(engagement_dir) answers from the record - the rules from the store's requests table, the four status fields from statuses, the keywords a filing taught from learned_keywords laid over the row's own Any Keywords by _with_the_record() - after store.follow_the_journal(); a folder with no journal is refused by NOT_AN_ENGAGEMENT. check_rules() is the warnings half of what the old manifest check said (a row with no rule, ANY_EXTENSION, a keyword with no letter or digit, a bare family number - decisions 55 and 58) and rides every state the app reads and every pass; there is no problems half, because a list the record holds was validated on the way in. Decision 120 took the atomic write out: the temp suffix, the temp path, the replacement context and the two writers over it are tracker/fsio.py at layer 0 now, and nothing is re-exported from here - this module owns the request list, not how a file is replaced. identifier_problem() refuses identifiers that could not survive as a folder-name prefix. with_statuses() is what the scanner uses to count the rows as it is about to leave them. Decision 62: derived_date_pattern() asks for the month a Period names. Decision 68: a status is matched to its row without case (records.identifier_key()). Decision 72: csv_tuple() takes a list as the list it already is; check_tax_year() is the one bound on a tax year. Decision 86: the details carry the form the list was cut from; create_engagement() takes it as a keyword because it is one fact about the engagement, and a blank never clears one the info carries. Decision 90: keyword_alternatives() lives here beside csv_tuple() because this module owns how a keyword is read - '|' names alternatives, '+' joins phrases wanted together. Decision 93: entity_keyword() is the one normalisation of an entity's name; narrowing_rows() says which rows narrow which and is empty for every shipped catalog; check_narrowing_names() refuses a list where one issuer name sits inside another's. The records it reads and writes - EngagementInfo, StatusUpdate, the rule row's serialisation - live in tracker/records.py (decision 100); RequestItem stays here because it is the schema of the list a person edits. What left with decision 104 - the workbook reader, the template writer, the slimming, the Engagement sheet's reader and writer, the manifest check - is set aside outside the tree in Retired - Excel manifest. Decision 116: the override is recorded with its reason and the second value is Override.NOT_APPLICABLE. override_reason is a rule field (records.RULE_FIELDS, last, so older rows read as blank), COLUMNS gains COL_OVERRIDE_REASON, and validated() refuses Accepted with no reason, the word OVERRIDE_REASON_OTHER itself, and a reason with no override; OVERRIDE_REASONS are the four one-click reasons. Override.RETIRED folds the retired spelling to its successor inside _override() on every read; item_from_record() is the ONE reader of a stored rule row (load_manifest, the save_rules diff's stored side, the API's editor rows), so a journal written before this decision is read as Not Applicable, its bytes are never rewritten, and saving an unchanged list records nothing. override_label() is the word people see - NOT_APPLICABLE_LABEL with the year detect_year() gives the row, or the bare value; the year is never stored. Summary.not_applicable replaces the old count. Decision 113 added the third write, and the only one that does not touch the rules a person typed: unlearn_keyword() takes back a keyword a filing taught one request, under the engagement lock, as one keyword_unlearned event through store.record() - journalled, not simply deleted, because deleting the store's row would be a fact only the database held and the next rebuild would put it back. Decision 128 added the twelfth column, Named: whether the document this request asks for carries a name. Blank is yes, everywhere a row is read without one - strict is the rule the owner asked for. Decision 137: WINDOWS_RESERVED_NAMES / is_reserved_name() (L6) - identifier_problem() refuses a device name; create_engagement() and a save_rules() that changes the link refuse a link that is not http(s) (L5, records.link_problem). nodes.role: Whose document is this: the matcher for the names a return's people put on their papers (decision 128). normalise() folds a name for matching - lower case, everything that is not a letter or a digit a space, padded so a phrase has boundaries; spelling_in() is that phrase test; propose_spellings() is what the app offers a person to tick for a name they typed; check_name() answers confirmed, another return's, or absent, with the spelling that decided it and the page it was on.
nodes.notes: Pure functions over text the caller already has: nothing here reads a file, takes a lock or knows what a return is. The check itself runs one layer up, in the filer's household pass, after the request lists have accepted a document and before the exactly-one rule; the router is untouched, because the router judges a request list and knows no person. A spelling is at least two words (records.MIN_SPELLING_WORDS): a family name alone is a whole phrase inside a company's name, so `Park` would confirm `Park Landscaping LLC`'s bank statement as the family's - the two-word rule is kept wherever a spelling is accepted and again in check_name(). Confirmed beats vetoed beats absent, so a joint page naming both spouses is confirmed for both returns and the exactly-one rule decides. Nothing is inferred: the app proposes and a person ticks, no spelling is ever learned from a document, and no fuzzy match is made. The CLI (python -m tracker.names "John A. Park") prints the proposals and records nothing.

nodes.role: The markup both of the firm's pages are drawn with, owned once: esc() (every value on either page goes through it), the table builder (header row in a thead, data in a tbody, headers optionally marked for a page that sorts them), Cell and Row for the few cells and rows that want a class, slug() for a word as a class name, unesc() for reading a value back out of an attribute, page_text() for the bytes a page is written as, and tolerant_console() for a console made to take what it cannot encode.
nodes.notes: Decision 91. It knows nothing about engagements, manifests or the record - values in, markup out - which is why it imports nothing from the package and both tracker/runner.py (the practice page, decision 75) and tracker/view.py (the engagement's own page) can import it without a cycle. There is deliberately NO helper for a script tag, a style sheet link or an image: a page naming the firm's clients must not reach the network to render, so a page's own style is inline in the module that owns that page. page_text() encodes with backslashreplace for the same reason the run log does - a name NTFS holds is not always one UTF-8 can, and one client's file name must not cost the whole page. api._slug is this module's slug(), so a status chip in the app and a status badge on the view are classed by one function. Decision 116: details() draws a folded block - a details element with an escaped summary over markup this module already drew - so the view folds its set-aside rows away with no script. Decision 108: tolerant_console() is the one home of the console guard - stdout and stderr reconfigured to replace what they cannot encode, where they can be reconfigured - and every command line that prints a client's file or folder name calls it before it parses a flag (rollover, filer, scanner, registry, review, scaffold, store, reminder, runner, router, content_check, view, ledger, validators; tests/test_single_source.py holds the list). It belongs here because this module already owns how text leaves the machine for a person and imports nothing from the package, so a command line at any layer can call it. It replaces characters and never swallows an error. The markup half is still exercised through the two pages that draw with it (tests/test_view.py, tests/test_runner.py); tests/test_page.py pins the console guard. Decision 118: PALETTE, FONT_SANS and FONT_SERIF live here too - the firm's colours by the design system's own primitive names, mirrored once because the app cannot read the design system at run time and Outlook cannot read a CSS variable. The reminder's HTML body carries the values inline and the desktop app reads them through the API's vocabulary, so neither the renderer nor the stylesheet writes a colour; tests/test_reminder.py pins every value and compares them with the design system's own tokens wherever they are readable beside the checkout.

nodes.role: Every refusal said once: for each cause, the note the scanner writes (a template), the marker the reminder recognises it by, the plain sentence the client is asked with, and whether the row is the firm's to look at.
nodes.notes: Replaced substrings retyped in reminder.py to recognise sentences typed in validators/content_check/scanner: rewording a producer silently changed what a client was asked. tests/test_reasons.py checks each marker is part of its own template and, since decision 121, of no other reason's: three sentences ended '; review manually' and that was UNCHECKABLE_TYPE's marker, so find() called a scan with no text layer an uncheckable file type; it keys on 'content rules cannot be checked' now, and find() is held to give every reason back from its own sentence whatever ALL's order. Decision 55: reasons_in() strips the file-name prefixes the scanner writes, so a marker is never found in a client's file name. OCR_FAILED is firm-side: ours to retry, not the client's to resend (decision 57). Decision 92 added NO_READABLE_TEXT (code 'unreadable', marker 'nothing in this file could be read'), which is the ONE reason here that is not a validation note: the router writes it into the index's Reason column when no word of a file could be read, and it is firm-side because the client's document may be perfectly good and only this machine cannot read it. It is in ALL, so find() and the review card's refusal words reach it like any other. Decision 93 added ISSUER_NOT_NAMED (code 'issuer-not-named', marker 'names none of them'), the second reason here that is not a validation note: the router writes it into the index's Reason column when a request list asks for a document one row per issuer and the document names none of them. Firm-side - the client sent the right document; a person files it or adds the row. Decision 109 added FILE_MOVED (marker 'not where the record put it') and COPY_CHANGED (marker 'not the one the record filed there'), a third kind again: the scanner writes them into a request's notes but does not decide them - it reads them off the rows the filer's sweep of the working copies recorded. Both firm-side with firm notes of their own, because the client sent the document and somebody here moved the copy or put another file in its place; both use the {listed} placeholder, so tests/test_reasons.py covers them with no new sample name. Decision 119 added INTERRUPTED_MOVE (marker 'an interrupted step meant to put') and INTERRUPTED_MOVE_LOST (marker 'an interrupted step was moving'), firm-side and {listed} like the other two: the filer's recovery writes them onto the row it could not finish as decided, and the scanner puts the row's own sentence in front of the request whose folder the file was going into. Decision 127 added two, both after UNREADABLE_PDF in ALL and each with a marker of its own: UNREADABLE_IMAGE ('not a readable image', the client's to send again) and HEIC_NOT_SUPPORTED ('HEIC reader installed', firm-side - the client sent an ordinary photo and the decoder is ours to install). Three sentences were amended, no marker among them: EXTENSION_NOT_ALLOWED's ask now offers 'a PDF, a photo or an Excel file', NO_TEXT_LAYER's says 'PDF or photo', and NO_TEXT_AFTER_OCR's dropped 'in PDF' because a photo reaches it too. Decision 137: TOO_LARGE (firm-side: a file past the size ceiling, never read) and the TEXT_CUT template, which explains a verdict on a cut text and is outside ALL. Decision 137 Part B: READING_STOPPED (the safety stop) and UNNAMED_ACROSS_HOUSEHOLDS (an unnamed document is never filed into another household), both firm-side. Decision 140: Reason.holds is its own property - whether a parked file carrying the reason holds the reminder (reminder._parked_holds, the one reader) - set on the eleven client-side reasons that held before and on SHOWS_ITS_FORM_NUMBER (code 'shows-form-number', marker 'but it shows the form number of'), which is firm-side and holds: the client's file may be fine, and asking for it again while it waits in review is the letter 117 exists to stop - and on its twin NAME_POINTS_AT (code 'name-points-at', marker 'but its file name points at'), the same near miss when only the file's name pointed. HOLDS lists them. Never read holds off firm_side again.

nodes.role: The record types every layer above names, and each one's own serialisation: IndexEntry with INDEX_LAYOUT (the index's columns, header and width per field), Evidence with the one cell format format_evidence() writes and parse_evidence() reads back, Routing (where one dropped file belongs and why), EngagementInfo with ENGAGEMENT_FIELDS / LABELS / HELP / NOTES, ENGAGEMENT_EDITABLE (the details a person may change in the app's editor) and DATE_FIELDS (which of them are dates), StatusUpdate, the rule row's RULE_FIELDS with rule_to_json() / rule_from_json(), entry_to_json() / entry_from_json() for a row as it is stored, ledger_key() for the identity a row is recorded under, and THE_RECORD - the phrase standing rule 2 is worded in. Person with PERSON_KINDS / PERSON_KIND_LABELS and the people list on EngagementInfo, name_parts() - the one way a name is cut into words - and RULE_NAME, the name tier's own rule of evidence (decision 128).
nodes.notes: Decision 100, the structural review's D4: each record lived in whichever module wrote it first, so a module that only wanted to NAME a row had to import the one that walks folders and takes the engagement lock to produce it. Nothing here reads a file, takes a lock or knows where an engagement folder is - values in, values out - which is why it imports nothing of the package at all and every layer above can name a record without loading its writer. tracker/manifest.py imports it, an in-layer edge and the only one that way round; tests/test_layers.py pins both halves. What did NOT move: RequestItem stays in the manifest because it is the schema of the list a person edits, made out of plain values with that module's defaults and validation, and means nothing away from it; FileError, FileReport and ContentResult stay where they are because they are one run's report of what it did, never stored. COL_IDENTIFIER is here rather than beside the manifest's other column headers because the request list and the index are joined by that header. The names a module still reads are re-exported from it (tests/test_records.py pins each as this module's own object); the manifest's copies of the details' field table and the yes/no words went with decision 104, because nothing read them from there. The store of decision 101 reads and writes these records from here, never from tracker/filer.py. Decision 102: THE_RECORD is here because standing rule 2 says a move is recorded in the record and the record is the journal and the store together. Decision 103: the rule half of a request row travels in the journal, so RULE_FIELDS and its two serialisers are here - the serialisation is a fact about the record, the parsing a fact about the list. Decision 104: ENGAGEMENT_EDITABLE names the details the editor may change (not the name - the folder is the name; not Rolled From - the rollover writes it; not the form - recorded once), and info_from_json() and the store's row reader hand the yes/no fields back as booleans, which the gate found they had not been while a workbook was the reader's source. Decision 109: as_pattern() is here - a note's template turned into the pattern that reads its own sentence back, every word escaped and every {name} the pattern given for it. It came from the scanner, which has read the regression sentence back this way since decision 108, because how a sentence the machine wrote is read is a fact about the shape it was stored in; the filer derives moved_to()'s pattern from the same function, so two readers share one derivation and neither retypes a word. It is why this module imports re, and it still reaches for nothing in the package. Decision 117: DATE_FIELDS is the one answer to which details are dates - the record's own serialisers, the API's reading of a wizard or editor spec and the editor's choice of box all read it instead of naming due, so the Filing Deadline added beside the Due Date cost one line in each. The deadline is the year's and the rollover clears it; the firm's phone is NOT a detail at all, because it belongs to the firm and not to an engagement. The two-word rule a spelling must keep is a fact about the record, so MIN_SPELLING_WORDS and is_a_spelling() live here and tracker.names matches with them; RULE_FLAG_DEFAULTS says what a yes/no field means when the line that wrote a row never said it, which is what makes a rule stored before decision 128 named. Decision 129 added Feed and the household's feeds: the return lines in other households a drop folder also feeds, written and read by their own functions (feed_to_json, feeds_from_json) so the journal's line and the store's column hold one shape. A feed naming no household or no return line is refused on the way back in (FEED_REFUSED), where the store's malformed-line guard sends a hand-edited journal's feeds to be judged.
