nodes.role: The orchestrator: walks Prepared/, runs the three validation tiers, resolves each row's status (override- and revert-aware), and RECORDS the result - one scanned event through store.record(), under the pass's lock, only for what changed. It never writes the request list (decision 103).
nodes.notes: Holds the per-engagement lock through engagement_lock() - the same context manager the filer uses - and reads the request list only once it has it, so a sort that finished in between is never invisible to the scan. Never touches the household's inbox at all. The lock itself lives in tracker.locking (ScanLockedError is an alias of EngagementLockedError). Reads each document through content_check.extract(), the same reading the router made of it as a drop, and usually finds the router's verdict already among the engagement's verdicts in the store; one PdfVerdictCache per scan. _resolve_status() is the status rule and _received_date() the Received-Date rule, named so _scan_item() reads as the three tiers and then the two decisions. A Received row whose Expected Count was raised says so instead of REGRESSION_FILES_CHANGED - decided on the pass the row leaves Received, when the record's count is still the Received one, and carried from the last note by _regression_why() on every pass after, because the regressed count would call every lost file a raised count (decision 108); a note with no regression sentence reads as REGRESSION_FILES_CHANGED. An Accepted row is written Received with a date (decision 33); ScanReport.summary is the one count. No Unfiled sheet: the index records parked files; ScanReport.warnings names loose files and unrecognised folders in Prepared/, and ScanReport.summary is summarize() over the rows as the scan leaves them. Decision 54's claim now rests on the record: the Received Date the last scan stamped is carried, not re-stamped, and a regression is measured from the status the record holds, because that is where a status is. Decision 103: _record_the_statuses() is the one write - one call, one transaction, and nothing at all when the pass found the engagement as it left it (ScanReport.recorded says how many). The scan calls filer.ensure() first, inside its own lock, so the store holds the engagement it is about to record to and the rules it works from are the ones the record holds (decision 104: the ones the app's editor last saved). Nothing but the record is written by a pass. Decision 58: a working copy the index says a person filed (ASSIGNED_BY_PERSON) is counted without the content rules (ACCEPTED_NOTE); the scan reads the index for that, and writes only the record and the engagement's verdicts in the store. Decision 60: a person's acceptance is the newest row for the location and its recorded bytes. Decision 62: a person's filing waives tier 2 too. Imports the filer's index reader at call time; the filer imports this module at call time inside _rescan() - the deliberate cycle, stated on the filer's node. Decision 109: the scan reads the index once (_the_index()) and acts on what the filer's sweep decided under the same lock - it writes no row of its own. _wandered() is the paths FILE_MOVED rows name as their copies' whereabouts, and _scan_item() drops those from a request's files before the tiers, because a mislaid copy is not the request's whatever its bytes say; _claimed_paths() is every working copy the record names, newest row per location, and a claimed path holding other bytes is _a_stranger_at(), written as reasons.COPY_CHANGED on the row and by _changed_copy_warnings() on ScanReport.warnings (decision 3 extended: the status is still what the files earn). A FILE_MOVED row whose home is under one of this request's folders writes reasons.FILE_MOVED. Both facts go in after FOLDERS_NOTE and before the failures, so the note's cut can never take a firm-side marker off the end, and neither is a failure - a moved copy leaves the request Missing, not Failed Validation. _filed_by_a_person() and the de-duplication hash through ContentCache.digest_of() now, so this module holds no sha256_of at all, and prune() keeps every file under Prepared/ rather than only what a request claims - a memo dropped for a parked copy or a stray was a file read again every pass. the pattern helper moved down to tracker/records.py as as_pattern(), where both readers of a written sentence share it; the regression read-back of decision 108 is unchanged. Decision 119: _interrupted() is the second thing the scan keeps out of a request's count - where a step that died half way was putting a working copy, and the sentence the row it parked carries. The wreck of a copy the power cut in half is nobody's document, so it is not counted and the row's own firm-side sentence goes on the request instead, which is what makes the request read Missing rather than Failed Validation for a document the client sent perfectly well.

nodes.role: Generates the Windows Task Scheduler XML or n8n workflow that runs tracker.runner unattended.
nodes.notes: One daily task is enough because the runner decides the drafting day. Recognizes Windows drive-letter paths as absolute even when generating from Linux. Decision 131: THE JOB NAMES NO CLIENTS ROOT - runner_arguments(settings_dir) writes -m tracker.runner --settings "<the app's settings folder>" --log (runner.SETTINGS_FLAG), and the runner reads the root from settings.json there at every run, so the root has one home and a root changed in the app is the root the job walks next; the Description names the settings file. ROOT_FLAG and the CLI's root option are gone; the CLI takes --settings, defaulting to this checkout's settings folder, and refuses one that names no clients root. The folder resolver is resolve_folder() now. install_task() registers the XML with schtasks (/f, so re-running changes the schedule); --install does both steps. The task name is the product name from settings.product_name(); the defaults (start, repeat, XML file name) are module constants the API's install-schedule reports back so the app shows what was actually installed. EXECUTION_TIME_LIMIT is locking.RUN_TIME_LIMIT_SECONDS rendered by iso_duration(), not a second number, because the lock's stale threshold is derived from the same limit. runner_arguments(frozen=True) is the packaged form of the one command line: the app's executable in runner mode (runner.RUNNER_MODE_FLAG) instead of -m tracker.runner, same arguments after it. TASK_NAME at import is safe because only the shell-launched API (or a source checkout) imports this module; the frozen job never does. Decision 55: quote_argument() doubles a trailing backslash so a drive-root clients folder survives the Windows argument parser.

constants.ROOT_IS_SYSTEM_DRIVE: '{root} is the whole system drive; the tracker would walk all of it. Choose the folder the firm keeps its clients in'
constants.ROOT_HOLDS_SETTINGS: "{root} holds the app's own settings and store ({settings}); choose the folder the firm keeps its clients in"
constants.ROOT_INSIDE_SETTINGS: "{root} is inside the app's settings folder ({settings}); choose the folder the firm keeps its clients in"
constants.ROOT_HOLDS_APP: '{root} holds the app itself ({app}); choose the folder the firm keeps its clients in'

nodes.role: The settings file beside the app (SETTINGS_FILENAME): the one place the clients root, the firm and the firm's telephone number are kept. clients_root()/set_clients_root(), firm()/set_firm(), firm_phone()/set_firm_phone(); product_name() reads app/package.json productName (or ENV_PRODUCT_NAME from the shell). ENV_SETTINGS_DIR from the Electron shell says where beside-the-app is. ENV_REAL_CORPUS and real_corpus_dir() name the other folder outside the repository: the firm's own redacted documents, with the expectations file's name and columns beside them.
nodes.notes: Replaced two roots (an env var for the app defaulting to a demo folder, a command-line path for the job) that nothing tied together. set_clients_root() refuses a folder that does not exist, so a typo cannot become an empty root the run walks for ever. The file is written through fsio.write_json_atomically() (decision 120; it was the manifest's until then, and that one import was the whole of this module's dependence on layer 1): the app and the scheduling CLI can both save it, and neither may swap the other's half-written temp into place. Decision 68: an empty root is refused - Path("") is the working folder. Decision 69: the working folder under any spelling is refused as a root. Decision 71: real_corpus_dir() answers None when the variable is unset and when what it names is not a folder, because raising would fail the suite on every machine that has no corpus, CI included; it is an environment variable rather than a setting because it belongs to a machine, never to an engagement. Decision 117: the firm's phone is a setting for the mirror image of that reason - it belongs to the firm and not to any one engagement, so it sits beside the firm's name rather than in every client's details, and it is taken as typed because a firm writes its number its own way. Only the reminder's final notice says it, and a blank one drops that sentence. Decision 131: the scheduled job names this file's folder (runner --settings) rather than the root, and reads the root from here at every run - one home for the clients root. Decision 137 (M3) replaced decision 69's working-folder check, which meant nothing in the packaged build: root_refusal() (pure, so every rule is testable on any OS) refuses the system drive's root (system_drive_root()), the settings folder, any folder holding it and any folder inside it, and the app's own folder (app_dir(): the frozen executable's, or the repository from source) and any folder holding it, each with its own sentence. Another drive's root is allowed - a letter mapped to the clients share is a real root - and "D:" is still recorded as "D:\\". Review fixes (decision 137): _inside() compares the folders themselves (os.path.samefile up the parent chain) as well as their spellings, so long-path (\\?\) and C$ admin-share forms are refused like plain names; clients_root_refusal() is what set_clients_root and the runner's start both ask.

constants.MALFORMED_LINE: '{where}: line {seq} of the record is malformed ({event} {problem}); the journal is not applied past it'
constants.REWRITTEN: "The record for {rel} was changed behind the tracker's back (line {line} onward no longer matches). Nothing was applied. Run the store check, then rebuild."

nodes.role: The store: one SQLite file per clients root (STORE_FILENAME) on the designated machine's local disk, beside the settings file, holding engagements, requests, statuses, learned_keywords, documents and events for every engagement under that root, all folded from the journal and from nothing else - and, since decision 107, the two tables of the tier-3 verdict cache, VERDICTS_TABLE and FILE_MEMOS_TABLE, which are NOT the record's: derived from the bytes and the rules, never journalled, left empty by a rebuild and never compared by check(). Owns the file name, the schema and its user_version (bumped by decision 104 when the workbook digest column left, by 107 when the cache's two tables arrived, by 116 for override_reason, by 117 for the Filing Deadline column and by 119 for the intents table), path_for(), open(), connect() / close() (one connection per process, to the file TRACKER_STORE names or the one beside the settings file), documents(), rules(), statuses(), learned_keywords() and engagement_info() (what the readers answer from), record() (the journal first, then one immediate transaction), sync(), catch_up() and follow_the_journal() (replay the lines the store has not applied, building the engagement from the journal alone where it has none; catch_up() is filer.ensure()'s, by count, and a look that finds nothing to apply takes no lock), rebuild_engagement() (delete and build again from the journal), cached_verdicts() and remember_verdicts() (the verdict cache's one read and one write - the write is its own immediate transaction under the engagement lock, never record()), forget() (drop a failed create's row), check() (every disagreement with the journal, as sentences), state() (current / behind / unknown, from the journal's head alone), export() (three CSVs on demand, every cell text, a cell that begins like a formula behind an apostrophe) and the CLI that rebuilds, checks, exports or states a whole clients root - its first argument read by store_named(): the app folder, the settings file in it, or the store file itself, and anything else refused so a typo never creates a store; a store open() refuses is said in its one sentence with exit 1, never a traceback (decision 107).
nodes.notes: Decision 101 built it and had nothing read it; 102 moved the index into it; 103 the statuses and the person's rules; 104 took away the last thing that was passed in from anywhere else. WHERE IT LIVES IS THE POINT: never under the clients root and never in an engagement folder, because those sync and a synced database file is a corrupted one - decision 87's finding, kept, with the owner's 2026-09-19 decision adding the local database the other side of that line. The journal stays in the folder and travels with the engagement; the store is local and disposable, and the arrow only points one way - the store is rebuilt from the journal, never the reverse. THE GUARANTEE is journal-then-apply: record() refuses outside the engagement lock and refuses a retired event name by sentence, appends each event through append() and only then folds them in one BEGIN IMMEDIATE, so a machine that dies between the two leaves the journal ahead and sync() replays the difference. The fold has one owner, apply() in tracker/ledger.py, so a line-at-a-time replay and a whole-file fold cannot differ. ONE CONNECTION PER PROCESS: connect() opens it on first use and every writer deep in the package asks for it by name; close() lets it go, which Windows needs before a database file can be deleted. TRACKER_STORE overrides where it is - the suite points every test at its own file. It imports records, ledger and locking and nothing else of the package at load time - narrower than its layer allows, so the database the readers answer from never depends on the modules that walk folders and move files; connect() reads tracker/settings.py at call time and the CLI imports the registry at call time to find the folders. The gate is check(), run by the autouse fixture in tests/conftest.py over every engagement the suite leaves behind: the documents and the rules are compared with ledger.replay() over the journal, always - an engagement with no rules event has none on either side - and the statuses and taught keywords with the same lines folded by the store's case rule (decision 136). Decision 104: the requests table is the fold of rules_changed (and of the rules_imported lines older journals carry, which _apply_rules_event folds the same way); rules() returns [] for an engagement the store holds and None only for one it does not; has_rules_event() is what a save is a difference from; rebuild_engagement() takes nothing but the journal (the workbook-fed fallback, the sequence number workbook rows were marked with, the digest column and its bookkeeping all went, and the schema guard that refused a request row whose fields had moved is a test in tests/test_store.py now); state() has one stamp, the journal's head, because a rules edit is an event; forget() is what a failed create leaves behind - nothing - and writes nothing to any journal. A version-1 file is refused by the sentence open() has always had, and is deleted and rebuilt: the store is disposable and no store at the office predates this chain. key_root() is the one rule for the key an engagement is stored under (root_for() is its name for a caller with no root in hand): the root the settings file names whenever the folder is under it - the record's own root, which wins over the root a caller typed, so a pass run on one client's folder and a check given the drive key the engagement as the app does - else the caller's root, else the root a return's position names (decision 134: four levels up, when its parent is a year folder and its household sits in the private tree, asked of layout at call time - so two years of one return are two rows on a machine or in a reader with no root in hand), else, only for a folder outside that layout, the folder's parent. _engagement_row() answers by that exact key, and under the recorded root by nothing else: a folder there with no row is one the store has not met, never another engagement whose key its path ends with (decision 106; the pre-integration audit found Clients/Archive/Smith 2025 answered as Clients/Smith 2025's row). The tail - the one stored path the folder ends with, longest wins - answers only where no recorded root covers the folder, which is decision 103's end-to-end finding on a machine with no settings file. Decision 107: the verdict cache's two tables are per engagement and cascade with it; cached_verdicts() returns the memos and the verdicts at the CACHE_VERSION the caller names as plain dicts and JSON text (this module never learns the verdict's record - test_layers pins that it imports nothing above it); remember_verdicts() deletes the rows at other versions, the paths and digests pruned, and upserts what was learned, refusing outside the lock and for an unknown engagement by the two sentences record() uses (_held_under_the_lock()). A version-2 file is refused by the same sentence a version-1 file was. RULE_COLUMNS is built from records.RULE_FIELDS; _rule_from_sql() hands the list fields back as lists and the flag as a boolean, the shape the API hands the editor. Decision 115: last_event() answers the newest event of a name for an engagement (or the newest carrying a key) from the events table - what the reminder compares this week's draft with, and what the runner reads the last draft day from. Decision 112: document_seqs() reads back what _apply() has always written - which journal line last wrote each index row - keyed through the recorded root as documents() is, {} for an engagement the store does not hold, no lock (a read). It is the freshness handle the app carries out with the row and a person's action carries back; per row rather than the engagement's head, so a scan between the card and the click refuses nothing. A rebuild numbers the same lines the same way, so the mapping survives it. Decision 113: _apply() deletes a learned_keywords row on a keyword_unlearned event, keyed by identifier_key and the keyword exactly, as the insert keys it; _check_learned() holds the table to ledger.Folded.learned - the table's words in seq order against the journal's fold, both sides folded through identifier_key first, one sentence per request that differs - and check() appends it, so the one part of this database the record could not vouch for is in the gate. _refuse_a_malformed_line() checks a keyword event for the first time: both events must name a request and a word, both text and neither blank, because a keyword that is not text was written into the table as the text of whatever it carried while the journal's fold kept the value itself, which is a disagreement the check would now report and nobody could act on. Decision 119: SCHEMA_VERSION 6 and the intents table - the fold of the moving lines, one row per key, holding the whole line - written by _apply() as each line is met and deleted by any row event naming the key (or by move_abandoned); open_intents() reads them back oldest first for the filer's recovery and for the refusal a person's action makes while one is open; _check_intents() holds the table to ledger.replay()'s own fold, so a rebuild gives the same open set and the gate would say which key they disagreed about; _refuse_a_malformed_line() learns the moving shape, because a recovery acts on it with a file already half moved, and (decision 126) the sharing_confirmed shape, which is no shape at all: that event carries nothing but its stamp, so a line of it carrying anything is another version's or a hand-written one and is refused by name rather than kept where a reader would trust it. The store's version did not move for it - it is folded by nothing and read back out of the events by last_event(). Version 8 (decision 128) added the return's people to engagements as JSON text and the named mark to requests; _to_sql writes a list with sorted keys, as the journal writes a line, so the column and the fold of the same people are one text and check() compares like with like. A rules_changed line whose people this version cannot read - an unknown kind, a one-word spelling - is refused by name before a value of it reaches a table. Decision 129 put the household's feed list into the household columns as JSON text and moved the schema to version 9; the malformed-line guard learned the feeds' shape. Decision 132 moved the schema to version 10 with no column change, because the fold changed: a released line (ledger.RELEASE_EVENTS) deletes the row under its key and closes its intent in _apply(), exactly as ledger.apply() does, and a version-9 file may hold Handed Over rows this version never produces. The guard requires a released line's key and refuses a row on it, and refuses a moving line carrying decision 129's also_in by name (ALSO_IN) - an intent whose second half this version cannot write must not be recovered as if it had none. Decision 134 moved the schema to version 11 with no column change, because the key changed: a version-10 file may hold two years of one return as one row, keyed by the return's name alone. DECISION 135, A READ NEVER OUTRUNS A WRITE: readers take no lock and the app's process and the pass's share the store, so every function that applies journal lines reads the row, the lines and the head inside its own BEGIN IMMEDIATE and takes the lines and the head from ONE read (ledger.read_with_head()): sync(), catch_up() (follow_the_journal()'s slow path and filer.ensure()'s) and record()'s apply through one helper, _catch_up(), and rebuild_engagement() through the same one read. A look that finds nothing to apply takes no lock: sync() and catch_up() first read the row and the journal outside any transaction and return when the applied seq already equals the journal's lines, and only a decision to write takes BEGIN IMMEDIATE and reads both again inside (_look_then_catch_up(); the look's parsed lines are reused there only when the file still digests to the look's head) - so the app's views, the Status Report and dry runs never queue a pass's record() behind the lock. A stored head therefore always names exactly the lines applied. record() applies what the journal holds past the store's applied_seq as it is inside the transaction, not the batch it was handed. follow_the_journal()'s head fast path stays outside any transaction and parses nothing; filer.ensure() calls catch_up(), which compares by count, so a store an earlier build left with a matching head and a short applied_seq (the stuck return: current by its head, every writer refused) is repaired by the next pass with no rebuild and no version change. Decision 136: check() folds the record's statuses and learned keywords from the journal's lines itself, keyed by identifier_key in journal order (_recorded_statuses, _recorded_learned), rather than taking ledger.replay()'s, which keys them by each line's spelling - so a request respelled by case is one request to the gate, as it is to the store. Decision 137 (L4): MALFORMED_LINE says "line N of the record is malformed"; _refuse_a_malformed_line() gained the ROW_EVENTS branch (a key that is text, a row that is a mapping, a was that is a location) and holds every rule's list fields to lists of words; _write_rule() and _rule_from_sql() hold them to the same shape where a row is written and read. Decision 137 (A3, store version 12): engagements.applied_digest holds the running chain over exactly the lines applied (ledger.read_with_chain / chain_at); _refuse_a_rewrite() proves that prefix in _look_then_catch_up's no-lock look (equal counts with a different chain refuses, never 'nothing to do'), in _catch_up, and in record() before it appends, with REWRITTEN; check() names it; the rebuild computes it. It never repairs itself: the check, then a rebuild.

constants.YEAR_NOTE: "Defaults to the most recently ended year; the checklist's periods follow it"

nodes.role: The per-form request catalog (FORM_TYPES, FORM_TEMPLATES): what each return type asks for and the keyword rules that recognise each document. The ONLY source of truth for the checklists; the wizard and the rollover read it directly. Since decision 117 it also holds the dates a form implies: FILING_DEADLINES with filing_deadline_for() (the statutory day in the year after the tax year, weekends shifted forward) and ask_by_for() (TARGET_DAYS_BEFORE_DEADLINE before it, moved back off the weekend).
nodes.notes: item_from_spec() gives a rule-less request its own document name as the required keyword, because a request with no rule can never auto-file, and the safe extension default. default_tax_year() is the calendar's most recently ended year; template_items(form, year=...) shifts the catalog's base year to it, relative periods included. No date_pattern in the catalog: each row's Period implies its year check. Decision 60: a catalog keyword is the form's own title or a phrase only it carries, never a word other forms print about it (a 1040 says W-2; a 1095-C says Marketplace). Decision 62: every catalog row keys on the document's own title phrase; tests/test_catalog.py routes reconstructions of the real forms against every catalog. Decision 63: the prior-year return rows require their form number and title, so a return wins over its schedules' lines. Decision 64: the return rows require their title phrase, not their number; the K-1 row keys on the K-1's title; tests/irs/ (the IRS's own forms) and tests/test_irs_forms.py route them all. Decision 65: every prior-year return row requires the jurat; schedule rows key on their titles, not on account names. Decision 66: no row keys on a line every return prints (dividends and distributions, ownership percentage, donation) or the organizer asks (child care provider); the receipt, list and childcare rows key on those documents' own titles. Decision 67: the receipt row does not key on contribution statement (an IRA's, a 529's); the childcare row knows the provider's statement; the estimated tax row keys on a voucher's own lines (its numbered heading, the amount line), not the booklet's prose. Decision 68: the receipt row keys on receipt wording only (a pledge, a thank-you and the firm's letter are not receipts); the estimated tax row knows the state voucher; the childcare row does not take an FSA administrator's statement. Decision 69: the receipt row keys on words only a charity prints; no form 540-es; L01 has no tuition statement (a checklist's line, a university's bill). Decision 72: item_from_spec() reads a spec's lists through manifest.csv_tuple(), the one parser, rather than a copy of it. Decision 73: the shared estimated-tax row is two rows, because an individual's 1040-ES voucher is not a corporation's record (business_estimated_tax keys on corporation estimated tax, estimated tax voucher, estimated payments made); the December bank row does not key on statement of account (a credit-card issuer's and a broker's heading) and takes a workbook, as the reconciliation it asks for arrives; the property tax row keys on the bill's own titles, not on assessor, parcel number or property tax bill (an assessor's notice and a servicer's escrow analysis print those); D01 drops thank you for your donation (every fundraiser's salutation); I01 drops advance payment of premium tax credit (a marketplace notice's sentence); J01 keys on child care/day care spellings with the run-together copies deleted, since the matcher reads the space as optional; 1041 A01 names the kind of trust (an IRA custodian's paperwork is a Trust Agreement too), B02 drops year-end account statement (a bank's heading), C01 drops distribution schedule (a mutual fund's), E01 knows stepped-up basis; 990 C02 keys on the schedule's own title rather than compensation of officers (Part VII's line and the Statement of Functional Expenses', which is now a financial statement's title), D02 on grants made rather than a bare grantee (a letter the charity received) or grants paid (the 990-PF's line 25), E01 without program description (a grant proposal's); the xlsx-only rows and the loans row take the format a client really sends, and officer_comp drops form 1125-e with it (the blank IRS form parks). Decision 85: 1040 E01 knows the wording a broker actually exports - realized gain/loss and the run-together realized gain loss beside the firm's own realized gain and loss - and takes a workbook, since that export arrives as an .xlsx as often as a CSV; 1041 B01 takes the same two, because the trust's realized gain/loss export is its 1099-B by another name. No IRS form in tests/irs/ says either word, and decision 68's consolidated 1099 never prints them, so the composite's placements are untouched. Decision 90, the owner's catalog: _prior_return() writes every prior-year return row's required keyword, with JURAT as the one owner of the line decision 65 added, and a state return's own printed title as an alternative inside that keyword - a standalone CA 540 or NY IT-201 files 1040 B01 on 'resident income tax return', a CA 568 or NY IT-204 files 1065 A01 on 'return of income + limited liability company' (both 568 heading lines, since decision 141) or 'partnership return', a CA 100S files 1120S A01 on 'franchise or income tax return', and another state is one more phrase, not a rule. The alternative lives inside the required keyword rather than in Any Keywords so the row's required set stays required: the prior-year return still outranks a row that matched on any keyword and one that fails another rule is still contested. The 1040 catalog gains A03-A06, one row per 1099 a person receives, keyed on the form's number - 'nonemployee compensation' is said by the IRS Attention page ahead of every information return and 'certain government payments' by the 1040-ES package, so neither is a keyword; 'miscellaneous information' and 'payment card' are, the second because the 1099-K's title never lands on one line and 'payment card' begins it, where a checklist's menu rule can see it. 'depreciation' joins SHARED - the 1120's C02 unchanged, 1120S F02 and 1065 D02 new - so the schedule behind Form 4562 has one set of words; a fixed-asset register that never says depreciation stays on fixed_assets, which all three catalogs already carry. Decision 93: the catalog keeps ONE K-1 row (1040 F01, K1_CATALOG/K1_IDENTIFIER) and it asks for the state K-1 too - California heads Schedule K-1 (568) "Member's Share of Income" - because which partnerships a client is in is a fact about that client, not about the 1040. issuer_row() cuts a row per issuing entity from k1_row(): same Any Keywords, same period and extensions, the normalised entity name in Required Keywords and in the Document. The 1065's F01 is Special Allocation Support; decision 141's H01 closes decision 85's F1 there. Decision 117, the owner's table: each form's statutory filing date lives here because it is a fact about the return type, like the checklist itself, and a form the table does not name gets no default date at all - a guessed deadline would be read out to a client in the firm's name. The weekend shift is the IRS's own rule; a holiday is a person's edit, because the federal and state calendars differ and move. Every catalog row carries a name mark since decision 128 - 61 of the 107 are named - and an issuer row is named because the K-1 row it is cut from is. Decision 141, the owner's rows: 1040 A07 (SSA-1099 / RRB-1099, required on the statements' own headings so it outranks E02, whose 1099-r the SSA's revision code 'SSA-1099-R-OP1' says), A08, A09, L02, L03 (required on the form number), M01 (the client's Schedule C sheet, any keywords on its own vocabulary) and N01; the business catalogs' K-1s received (required on the partner's, beneficiary's and member's K-1 titles, never the S corporation's, which no business can hold and whose title the S-corp return prints), 1099-K / 1099-NEC received and 1042-S rows; the 1041's G01 carries the estimated_tax title but files only a 1041-ES (an individual's 1040-ES parks there), the one row tests/test_templates.py lets carry a shared title with rules of its own; A08 wants the 1099-C's words beside its number, since OCR reads 1099-G as 1099-C; M01 keys on the summary's shape (gross sales + ending inventory + total expense), never a mileage line; and Z01, the notices row, last on every catalog, keyed on the current IRS notice header (notice date with tax year or tax period, with the agency) and narrow on purpose. The 1042-S, K-1-received, business 1099 and notices rows are SHARED entries.

nodes.role: Tiers 1-2: does the file exist, is the extension allowed, is it big enough, is the PDF readable and - since decision 127 - does the photo open. Pure read-only functions plus passive cloud-placeholder detection for OneDrive and Google Drive.
nodes.notes: DECISION 127 - A PHOTO IS A SCAN: IMAGE_EXTENSIONS (jpg, jpeg, png, heic, heif, tif, tiff) is accepted by every request that accepts a PDF, through _extension_allowed(), so no catalog row and no stored rule changed and a request list recorded before the decision admits photos the day it lands; a row that names an image type itself is taken at its word, and a row listing xlsx/csv alone refuses a photo with the sentence it always refused it with. DEFAULT_EXTENSIONS is untouched. At tier 2 a photo gets from _image_error() what a PDF gets from _pdf_error(): Image.open() + verify(), no pixels decoded, nothing written - a file Pillow will not open is reasons.UNREADABLE_IMAGE (the client's to resend), and a HEIC on a machine whose decoder is missing is reasons.HEIC_NOT_SUPPORTED (firm-side, never an ask: they sent an ordinary photo). pillow_heif.register_heif_opener() runs once at import inside a try, and HEIC_READABLE says whether it did; there is no PdfVerdictCache-style memo because verify() reads a header. Never downloads a cloud-only placeholder — a stub must never be filed as if it were the document. A file that vanishes between listing and stat is reported pending_sync, never raised — a scheduled scan must not die on one replaced file. PdfVerdictCache is a run's memo of PDF readability (the router asks once per manifest row for one file; the scanner asks again): the filer and the scanner each make one and pass it down, so nothing is shared at module level between runs that might one day be concurrent. UNFINISHED_SUFFIXES is the one list of transfer-in-progress names (decision 56). Decision 137 (M5): MAX_READ_MB (250) and TEXT_READ_CAP_MB (20) sit here as constants, not settings; too_large_reason() is what the router and the reader ask before a file is opened.

constants.VIEW_NOTE: 'This page is regenerated every pass and holds no facts of its own: every value on it comes from the record, the request list and the index.'

nodes.role: The page a person opens: VIEW_FILENAME, regenerated in the engagement folder at the end of every real pass from the readers (load_manifest() for the request rows and their statuses, read_index() for the originals, review.triage() for what each parked file might be), in four sections - Summary, Requests, Index, Needs Review. Owns the file name, the Summary's labels and their meta names, the three words a view's state is said in (CURRENT / BEHIND / UNKNOWN), the chip's label and the button's, render_page(), write_view(), view_state(), read_stamp(), the two row builders (request_row(), index_row()) and the CLI that redraws one engagement and prints its state.
nodes.notes: Decision 89, stage A step 3, as decision 91 settled it: the owner's rule is that every file staff open only to READ is a web page. IT HOLDS NO FACT, and that is the whole design: no fact is read back - only the stamp in its meta tags, by read_stamp(), for the current / behind / unknown chip - so the one failure every other file must survive costs nothing here. A page whose replace does not land is not replaced, the run carries view_stale and SUCCEEDS, the older page stands and the next pass lands one. Written through manifest.write_text_atomically(); there is no read-only attribute (a browser holds no write lock). On Windows a plain open() read handle still refuses the replace, so view_stale has a real trigger there. Every value goes through page.esc() and the page fetches nothing. The stamp lives in meta tags in the head and read_stamp() reads it with one regular expression - no HTML parser in production. Decision 104: view_state() compares ONE digest - the record's head (ledger.head()) as it was when the page was drawn, against the head now; a rules edit is an event, so an edit moves the head and the page is honestly behind, and the workbook's digest that used to be the second stamp is gone with the workbook. Section headings come from their owners (REQUESTS_SECTION here, filer.INDEX_HEADING, filer.NEEDS_REVIEW) and the review shortlist's sentences from tracker/review.py. Imports downwards only - ledger, manifest, filer, review, page - and only runner and api import it; writing the view is the last thing a pass does. tests/conftest.py draws the page again from the live readers through render_page() after every test and requires the same bytes, with only the clock excluded. Decision 103: this page is where the statuses and the Validation Notes are READ: REQUEST_COLUMNS is the manifest's ten plus the four the record holds, side by side, and a keyword a person's filing taught the row is in Any Keywords beside the ones they typed.

nodes.role: Electron main process. Spawns the Python API (`python -m tracker.api`, or the frozen executable package.json's config.apiName names in the portable build) and relays its JSON to the renderer over IPC.
nodes.notes: This is the cross-language boundary: everything the UI can do is a tracker.api command. The renderer is untrusted here: a command must be in vocab.commands (before the vocabulary arrives, only BOOTSTRAP_COMMAND, pinned to tracker.api.COMMANDS by a guard) with the one argument shape the renderer uses; open-path opens only a path the API reported in state.paths; the tracker's exit code is read, not discarded, and a tracker that outlives TRACKER_TIMEOUT_MS is killed and reported. The window is sandboxed, cannot navigate and cannot open windows.

nodes.role: Context bridge exposing only the calls tests/test_single_source.py checks against main.js.call(args, payload), tracker.open(path) and tracker.pickFolder(). Nothing else crosses.

The desktop UI: the form-type wizard, the request list and the scan results, and (decision 104) the request-list editor - the only place a rule is entered. Talks only to window.tracker from the preload bridge.
nodes.notes: Every node is built with el() and placed with replaceChildren; there is no innerHTML and no escaper, so a client's file name, a keyword somebody typed into the request list or a folder name is text whatever characters it carries (a guard checks the sinks are absent). Every word it shows or compares comes from the API's vocabulary (applyVocabulary); SCAN_LABEL is the one label it owns. Decision 76: the Needs Review card asks one question of a parked and a set-aside document alike - which request does this belong to - so reviewRow() builds both, and only an open question carries the note box and the button that sets one aside; what a person has set aside is folded under its own count, never removed from the page, because the list is the only way back. Decision 77: renderUnfileList() is the same list for what is already filed - folded away, there for the one row that is wrong - and the function cannot be called after the decision it shows, because the guard on the renderer's vocabulary forbids that word anywhere in the file. Decision 84: the Needs Review card shows the shortlist. renderReview() maps state.review by pbc_location and hands each parked row its triage; reviewRow() puts the shortlist at the head of the picker under the 'suggested' heading, every other request under 'other_requests', and lists the sentence behind each suggestion beneath the row - an <option> carries no second line, and the reason is what is read before anything is picked. The picker starts on the best suggestion, falling back to the router's own first candidate. A parked file the evidence says nothing about shows the vocabulary's nothing_suggested rather than a guess, and a set-aside row is not triaged at all, so it gets no shortlist. Every word of it - the two headings and the File it label as well - comes from vocab; the renderer still types none. Decision 89: a chip beside the engagement's name says whether its own page still describes it. The word and the label are the API's (vocab.view), the chip's class is derived from the word the same way a status chip's is, and the button opens state.paths.view through the same whitelisted opener the Open Status button uses. Decision 91: that button's label is the API's too - applyVocabulary() fills #view-label from vocab.view.open, exactly as it fills the scan button - so the page carries no word for it, and the path it opens is now an .html file the shell hands to the default browser. Decision 104: requestRows() is the one row component - a table of inputs built from vocab.columns (each column's key, header and help; the two numbers as number inputs whose minimum comes from vocab.editor.minimums, the override a pick of vocab.overrides), used by the wizard's custom-request section (three columns, identifiers assigned as rows are added) and by the editor (all ten). openEditor() opens on state.rules - the person's rows as stored, a derived date pattern shown blank, the file types shown as '*' when any - with the engagement's details laid out from vocab.editor.engagement_fields (a text box, a date or a yes/no box for the editable ones, plain text for the rest) and the keywords filings taught shown beside each row as taught (vocab.editor.learned_note), never as typed. pasteRows() appends rows pasted from a spreadsheet by position - tab-separated if any line holds a tab, otherwise CSV through a small RFC 4180 reader, a first line that repeats the headings skipped - and records nothing. saveEditor() is one edit call: a refusal is shown inside the editor with its row and column and the modal stays open; a save renders the state the API returns, closes, and says what changed or that nothing did, with the warnings under vocab.editor.warnings_heading. Every heading, label, hint and button of the editor is vocab.editor's or vocab.columns'; the Check Manifest button and the button that opened the workbook are gone with the workbook. Decision 112: both row builders put the row's sequence number on the <li> (dataset.seq, from state.index[].seq and state.review[].seq) and assignParked(), dismissParked() and unfileDocument() send it back as seq; assignParked's banner shows the API's overrode_shortlist sentence as a warn note beside left_in_review. A refusal goes through refused(): the API's sentence is toasted, the button re-enabled and refresh() re-reads the state, so the card shows the row as the record now holds it. The renderer types no sentence of its own here either. Decision 113: the learned cell is a list rather than a line - learnedCell() draws the API's learned_note and then one span.ed-learned-word per taught keyword, each with its own button.ed-unlearn carrying the identifier and the word - and a click calls the unlearn command, then re-draws only the learned column from the state that comes back (renderLearnedCells), because unlearning is its own event and lands at once while the rows may hold edits the person has not saved. The note area says the API's unlearned_note, and its scan_note under it when the re-scan could not run; the renderer types no word of it. Decision 110: renderMoved() draws #moved-card above the review card from state.moved - one row per moved working copy, its home and where its bytes are now, with restoreMoved (the restore command), keepMoved (assign, with the request the picker was left on and the keyword typed) and reviewMoved (unfile) behind the three buttons, delegated on #moved-list. The picker and the keyword box are shown only where the API said which request's folder holds the copy, and the picker starts on it; every word is vocab.review_labels', including the word for a copy that is nowhere. Decision 114: renderReview() draws the same queue twice - the list in #review-list and, in #review-deck, one card at a time. renderDeck() builds the deck from state.review in the API's order with the rows a person sent to the back after it (skipped, pbc_locations, dropped as soon as a row leaves the queue), shows the first card, and is called again from every render, so a row filed or set aside anywhere else simply leaves the deck and the total is always the queue's. The card shows the row's reason, the top suggestion's sentence under the list's own 'suggested' heading (or the vocabulary's nothing_suggested), the set-aside sentences, a keyword box and the position line; acceptCard() files to the suggestion the card carries, openCardInList() switches to the list and outlines the row, skipCard() reorders and sends nothing. fileRow() is the one place the assign call is made - assignParked(), acceptCard() and keepMoved() all reach it, and a guard in tests/test_single_source.py keeps it the only one, so Accept and File it cannot drift apart. reviewMode is the person's choice of rendering, read and written in localStorage under REVIEW_MODE_STORAGE_KEY inside try/catch (a blocked store leaves the app on the list); it is a key and not a word, and nothing about the deck is recorded (decision 83). Decision 118: renderReminder()/loadReminder()/drawReminder() are the Reminder card - the record's last word on the draft, the four stages as a toggle coloured from the API's palette, the letter drawn from its own shape with el() (never from the clipboard's markup, which would be an HTML string), Copy for Outlook putting text/html and text/plain on the clipboard with the same words, Approve sending back the fingerprint of the text on screen, and Open the draft file on the path state.paths names. The stage a person picked is the only thing the page holds of its own and is dropped when the engagement changes. It types no colour: every hex it draws with is looked up in vocab.reminder.palette by the key a stage carries, and a guard reads the file for one. Decision 129 added the household card's two feed lines, the editor's feed list with its picker and its warning, and File under another return on both renderings of the queue - every word of it from the API's vocabulary, as always.

nodes.role: Desktop app shell markup: empty placeholders the renderer fills from the API's vocabulary, under a Content-Security-Policy that allows nothing but the app's own files. Since decision 104 it holds the request-list editor's modal (#editor), every label of which the renderer fills, and the Edit Request List button (#btn-edit) that opens it; the min of a number input is never typed here.

nodes.role: How the day-to-day workflow runs.
What Build App.bat installs: requirements.txt plus the pinned PyInstaller.
Runtime and dev dependencies, pinned exactly (a guard refuses a range); the optional OCR extras are documented here too.
nodes.notes: requirements-build.txt adds the pinned freezer on top for Build App.bat; api_entry.spec is the committed freeze and app/package-lock.json the committed Electron install, so a build is made from the commit rather than from whatever was current that day (decision 46).

nodes.role: Builds the portable package: freezes the API with PyInstaller from the committed api_entry.spec inside a virtual environment holding exactly requirements-build.txt, packages the Electron shell with @electron/packager, copies the frozen API into resources/ and writes BUILD-INFO.txt.
nodes.notes: Reproducible from the commit (decision 46): the freeze runs in its own venv because PyInstaller follows optional imports and the machine's Python would otherwise leak unrelated packages into the package (decision 53). The packager runs through its entry script under `node`, not the `npx` shim, for the ampersand reason Start App.bat states; the copy into the package is `robocopy` with its exit code checked and the executable's presence asserted, because `xcopy` gave up on the package's long paths while the script still reported success (decision 53). Guards pin OUT to .gitignore and the resources path to app/main.js. Decision 55: the venv is made fresh each build; no parenthesised value is expanded inside the build-info block. Decision 78: every exit goes through one `:wait` label, which pauses for the person who double-clicked unless TRACKER_BUILD_NONINTERACTIVE is set - the one switch, named in this file's header and read nowhere else, and what lets .github/workflows/build.yml run this file rather than a copy of it.

nodes.role: Runs the desktop app from source: checks for Python and Node, installs the Electron packages app/package-lock.json pins (`npm ci`, first run only) and starts Electron.
nodes.notes: Electron is started through its own entry script under `node`, never the `npx` shim: the shim breaks when the folder's path contains an ampersand, which the firm's own checkout does (decision 53). Electron downloads its binary on the first start, so the install step needs the network once. Decision 55: installs requirements.txt every start (a second when satisfied).

nodes.role: PyInstaller entry point: the portable app's one executable, which is the tracker API by default and the scheduled job (tracker.runner.main) when RUNNER_MODE_FLAG comes first.
nodes.notes: PyInstaller needs a real script, not a -m module. Runner mode is dispatched before tracker.api is imported, because the API imports tracker.scheduling whose TASK_NAME needs the product name the Electron shell passes in the environment - and Task Scheduler passes nothing; the job needs neither of the shell's variables. api_entry.spec (committed; reads config.apiName from app/package.json) is how it is frozen.

nodes.role: The firm's Command Center integration surface, and the whole of it: the card this tool shows on the office dashboard, and the four actions it offers there - a preview pass, a real pass, the engagement list and the learned keywords. No tracker code reads this file; the Command Center discovers it under its configured roots and runs the argv arrays in it with cwd set to the repository root.
nodes.notes: Decision 81. The Center's safety contract refuses any manifest declaring that it schedules itself, and refusing one never stopped a Task Scheduler entry - it only meant this tool stayed off the board or declared a falsehood. The owner's written exception of 2026-09-18 is declared here in safety.scheduled_exception, the dated field the contract gained the same day, and the card prints that sentence; auto_send and money_movement admit no exception, ever. Each action is an argv array, never a shell string, and every flag it names has to exist in the module it calls. The pass takes the clients root as a positional argument rather than reading settings.py, because Task Scheduler and the Center hand the process none of the shell's environment - api_entry.py's rule: the job needs nothing but its command line; tools/learned_keywords.py takes no parameter here and reads the root from the settings file itself. run-pass carries the log flag ahead of a bare -- so the root that follows is read as the positional and not swallowed as the log's optional value.

nodes.role: Puts the repo root on sys.path so tests can `import tracker` without installing the package - explicitly now, beside pyproject's pythonpath, for editor runners and pytest's rootdir detection.
The firm-side working set: renamed copies sorted per request, plus 00 - Needs Review for anything that could not be identified. The client never sees this.

The page a person opens (decisions 89 and 91), in the engagement folder beside the record, and the only file there without a leading underscore because it is the one staff are meant to open. One self-contained HTML file - inline style, no image, no font, nothing fetched - with a sticky navigation and four sections: Summary (the record's head, when it was drawn in UTC and in local time, the counts, and the sentence that says it holds no facts of its own), Requests (statuses as coloured badges; since decision 116 the rows set aside as Override.NOT_APPLICABLE are not in the table but folded below it in one page.details() block per year, headed NOT_APPLICABLE_SECTION with the label and the count, dimmed, in the same columns - and Override Reason is a column), Index and Needs Review (the parked rows, each with the shortlist review.triage() computes and one line per set-aside row it names). Every table sorts on a click through a few lines of inline script and is a plain table without it. REGENERATED BY EVERY REAL PASS from the readers, never on a dry run. It HOLDS NO FACT - every value on it is the record's - so no fact is read back (read_stamp() reads only the stamp) and there is nothing on it to edit. The stamp is in meta tags in the head (tracker-record-sha256, tracker-generated and one per Summary field), which view_state() reads with a regular expression; since decision 104 the stamp is the record's head alone, because a rules edit is an event and moves it. A page whose replace does not land - on Windows an open read handle is enough to refuse it - is simply not replaced: the run reports view_stale and succeeds, and the one on disk stays honestly behind. The app says current / behind / unknown beside the engagement's name (tracker.view.view_state) and opens it with the Open Status Report button; `python -m tracker.view <folder>` redraws one.

The engagement's own append-only record (decision 87), in the engagement folder beside the client's files: one JSON event per line, in the order the writers wrote them - what was preserved, filed, parked, called a duplicate, decided by a person, had its bytes recorded, taught a keyword, the statuses each scan applied, and (decision 104) the request list and the engagement's details as the app's editor saved them, one rules_changed event per save carrying exactly what moved. Written only under the engagement lock, with O_APPEND and fsync, one line per event and never rewritten; a torn last line is ignored by the reader and truncated by the next append. Since decision 102 it is the whole of the index, since 103 the whole of the statuses, and since 104 the whole of the person's rules: filer.read_index(), manifest.load_manifest() and manifest.load_engagement_info() all answer from the fold of these lines (through the store, which keeps the fold so no reader pays for it twice), and there is no other copy. Its presence is what makes a folder an engagement (tracker/registry.py). A journal from before decision 104 may carry rules_imported and migrated lines; both are folded and neither is ever written again. A record that does not read as one is refused by name and the line, for every reader. A person never edits it, and `python -m tracker.store <store> check <root>` is how a person checks the database against it.
The drafted chase email, waiting for a person to read, edit and send. Carries a fingerprint so the weekly job can tell whether it has been edited.

The one run log in the clients root (LOG_FILENAME in tracker/runner.py): one summary line per pass, appended by a pass run with the log flag - the scheduled task and the Command Center's run-pass action both pass it - never on a dry run, and never read by the system; a person opens it.

The practice on one page, in the clients root beside the run log: every engagement with what it owes, the review queue across all of them newest first, and everything that failed. Written by every real pass (STATUS_PAGE_FILENAME in tracker/runner.py) and by the app's own pass; read by a person, who opens it from the clients folder or with the app's Open Status button. One self-contained file - no script, nothing fetched - because it names client files. Never on a dry run.

nodes.id: artifact:the client's folder for the year
nodes.role: Clients/<Household>/<YYYY>/ - where an original rests after the pass moves it out of the inbox, in the tree the client is shared (decision 125). Flat: one folder per year per household, not sorted by return or by request, because the original's resting place is the record's identity for the document and an original moves exactly once.

The household's one permanent drop folder, in the tree a client is shared (decision 125) — the only thing they touch. One per household however many returns it has. Their originals end up in the household's folder for the tax year, beside it, still visible to them and untouched; nothing under that tree is ever a record, a lock, a working copy, a draft or a page.

The store (decision 101): one SQLite file per clients root, on the designated machine's local disk beside the settings file, holding every engagement's requests, statuses, learned keywords, index rows, details and journal events under that root - all folded from each engagement's journal and from nothing else - and, since decision 107, the tier-3 verdict cache (the verdicts and the file memos), which is the one thing in it that is not a derivation of the journal: a rebuild leaves it empty and the next pass reads each document once. NEVER under the clients root and never in an engagement folder - those sync, and a synced database file is a corrupted database file. Written by tracker/store.py, and through it by the filer, the scanner and the manifest's two writes; read, through the store, by every reader of the index, the request list and the details. Disposable all the same - delete it and every fact it held is still in the journals - so it is never backed up, never synced and a person never opens it. One connection per process (connect(), close()), to the file beside the settings file unless TRACKER_STORE names another; the suite sets that per test. At the user_version `tracker/store.py` declares as `SCHEMA_VERSION`, raised by decisions 104 (the workbook's digest column went), 107 (the verdict cache's two tables), 116 (`override_reason`), 117 (the Filing Deadline column) and 119 (the `intents` table); a file at any other version is refused by name rather than opened, and an earlier one is deleted and rebuilt from the journals.

The pile of client documents the suite starts from, built from nothing: text_pdf() prints lines to a real one-page PDF, sheet_xlsx() writes rows to a real workbook, and build_samples() assembles the drop folder a client would leave (a duplicate, last year's form, a Word file, a Google Sheets shortcut, a photo, a half-uploaded temp file).
nodes.notes: No fixture files in the repository and no client data, so every test starts from the same pile. It was the marketing demo's sample builder in tracker/api.py; the demo went (decision 41) and the suite still needed the pile. listing_denied() makes a folder really unlistable for the running account, because rglob and os.walk reach the file system by different calls and a monkeypatch of one proves nothing about the other. Decision 73: sheet_xlsx() is how tests/test_catalog.py routes its workbook cases - half of every catalog asks for a schedule a client keeps in Excel, and a sheet is read as rows of tab-separated cells (a phrase across two cells is one phrase, a phrase down two rows is two labels), so typing one as prose would prove the wrong reading. Decision 78: build_scratch_root() assembles the same pile into a whole clients root - one scaffolded engagement with the documents already dropped - which is what .github/workflows/build.yml runs the frozen package over; the fixture lives beside the pile rather than in a tool of its own so there is one pile and not two that drift. It records the engagement through manifest.create_engagement() directly rather than through the suite's helper, because the build workflow imports this module without conftest (decision 104). openpyxl is imported here to WRITE a client's spreadsheet for the suite to read, which is the one use of it the tree keeps. The pile's 'file nobody accepts' is a .bmp since decision 127: it was a .jpg until a photo became a document, and the claim it carries is about a file type no row takes.

nodes.role: Guards the backtest: a document is routed by its text and never by its name, a file with no text layer is counted apart rather than parked, the report and the console carry no file or folder name, the skeleton is blank with the request folder as the hint and is never overwritten, and an unrecorded baseline is said rather than passed.
nodes.notes: Decision 74. The corpus it scores is built with tests/samples.py in a temporary folder, because no client document is in the repository or ever will be. It also pins the two things the hiding rests on: the neutral name reaches no keyword in any shipped catalog, and a whole pass writes nothing under the repository root.

nodes.role: Guards what only the build workflow could otherwise discover ten minutes into a release: that it runs the batch file the repository owns rather than a copy of the build, that the switch it sets is the one that batch file reads, that the flags it fires at the frozen executable are flags tracker/runner.py declares, that it passes the two environment variables tracker/settings.py names, and that both workflows quote the one interpreter pyproject.toml writes down.
nodes.notes: Decision 78. It also asserts the fixture: a scratch root is one engagement discovery finds and a whole dry pass walks, because a smoke check over an empty folder proves only that discovery does not crash. Nothing here can prove the package runs - only the Windows runner can. Decision 137 (M5): constraints.txt pins the whole tree the portable build freezes; the suite holds requirements*.txt to it, "Build App.bat" to installing with -c constraints.txt, and every BUILD-INFO.txt under build-portable/dist to freezing nothing else.

The clients roots are scratch trees under tmp_path, built the way tests/test_registry.py builds one: tests/conftest.py's make_engagement() records the shipped catalog through create_engagement() and a keyword_learned event teaches the keyword, so what the report compares is a real record rather than a stand-in. nodes.role: The harness for the firm's own redacted documents: every row of the expectations file beside them routed against a shipped catalog the way tests/test_irs_forms.py routes the IRS's forms, and asserted to file where the firm says or to park.
nodes.notes: Decision 71. The corpus is outside the repository, in the folder TRACKER_REAL_CORPUS names, and is never committed; with no corpus the routing case skips by name and the harness's own tests - the reading, the routing and the skip - still run on a scratch folder, so the file is exercised on every machine. nodes.notes: Decision 74. The measure the fifty blank IRS forms and the typed cases cannot be - decision 70's report leaves most keywords and most rows defended by nothing - and the only corpus made of documents a client actually sent. Each document is routed through a hard link (a copy where the file system refuses one) under one neutral name, so the router's by-name fallback can never read the client's name off the file and the score is the routing rules' rather than the firm's naming discipline; the link is the same bytes, so every tier-2 check still sees the real document. A document with no text layer is its own category, because the only evidence left for it would be the name being hidden - unless OCR is allowed, when nothing is handed over and the router does its own reading under its own stricter rule for OCR words. Catalogs are built the way tests/test_irs_forms.py builds them, with the size floor and the year check lifted. Nothing identifying comes back: counts, catalog identifiers and a row's number in the expectations file, never a file name, a folder name below the corpus root or a word of a document; the corpus, its expectations file and the report stay outside the repository and the tool refuses to write into the tree. Decision 127: route_one() also says which of READING_KINDS each document got - text, ocr or image - and the report's timing carries readings_by_kind, so the reader benchmark can say what a photo costs without a folder of text-layer PDFs flattening the number. The rule is unchanged: an image needs OCR_FLAG, exactly as a scan does.

nodes.role: Lists what the staff taught the router: every keyword a person taught one engagement's request that no catalog row with the same identifier and document carries, across every engagement under the clients root, grouped by request row with the number of engagements that typed it.
nodes.notes: Decision 79. A keyword a filing teaches lives in that one engagement's record, so fifty engagements hold fifty private vocabularies and the catalog is the only one tests/test_catalog.py and tests/test_irs_forms.py defend; this is the season's list of candidates to promote. Read-only in the strong sense: no lock is taken, nothing in an engagement folder is written or moved, and a report path inside the repository is refused - an engagement folder name is a client's name and the report names them on request. The engagement's details have recorded the catalog form since decision 86, but this tool does not read it: a row is compared against every catalog holding it and the report says which matched; a row no catalog holds is a custom request, listed apart with all its keywords. An engagement whose record could not be read is a problem line, never a silent skip. It borrows shipped_catalogs() and corpus_documents() from tools/vocab_report.py, so the catalogs it compares against - built through manifest.validated() over template_items() since decision 104 - and the corpus a candidate can be run over are the coverage report's. manifest_rows() reads through manifest.load_manifest(), which is what puts a taught keyword in front of any reader at all.
